trials.response:
**Short answer: Yes, it can be legal, but only as a regulated "high-risk" AI system with the obligations met.** It is not banned. It is also not a free yes. A bare "yes" would be bad advice, because several common setups of this exact tool are unlawful from day one.

The AI Act is an EU regulation, so it applies the same way in Germany and France. What differs between the two countries is labour law and data-protection practice, and those decide whether you can actually switch the tool on.

## Why it isn't a plain yes

- **The Act names CV ranking explicitly as high-risk.** Annex III, point 4(a) covers AI used "to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates."
- **The Article 6(3) exemption won't help you.** That exemption is for narrow or preparatory tasks, but an Annex III system that profiles people is always high-risk. Ranking candidates on their CVs is profiling.
- **GDPR, anti-discrimination law and German and French labour law also apply.** They apply right now, whatever happens to the AI Act deadlines.

## It's a "no" if any of these are true

| Situation | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| The tool reads emotions from video or voice interviews, or uses biometrics to infer race, religion, sexual orientation, political views or trade-union membership | These are prohibited practices under Art. 5(1)(f) and (g), banned since 2 Feb 2025. Fines go up to EUR 35M or 7% of global turnover. |
| Low-ranked candidates are rejected automatically and nobody meaningfully reviews them | This breaches GDPR Art. 22 (solely automated decisions). Since the CJEU's SCHUFA ruling (C-634/21), a score that the decision-maker relies on heavily can count as the decision itself, so a rubber-stamp "human in the loop" doesn't protect you. It also breaches the AI Act's human-oversight duties. |
| You built the tool in-house, or recruiters rank CVs by pasting them into a general-purpose LLM (ChatGPT, Copilot, etc.) | You become the **provider** of a high-risk system (Art. 25). That brings full provider obligations: conformity assessment, technical documentation, CE marking and EU database registration. Ad hoc LLM ranking almost never meets them. |
| Germany: the works council hasn't agreed | Use requires co-determination under BetrVG §87(1) no. 6 and §95 (selection guidelines; §95(2a) explicitly covers AI). The works council can get an injunction to stop the tool. |
| France: the CSE hasn't been consulted, or candidates weren't told in advance | CSE consultation on new technology (Code du travail L2312-8) is required before rollout. French courts have suspended AI deployments, including ones labelled pilots, when this step was skipped. L1221-8 and L1221-9 require you to tell candidates beforehand which recruitment methods you use. |
| The vendor can't give you AI Act documentation | You can't meet your deployer duties without the provider's instructions for use, logs and conformity documentation. |

## What makes it a "yes"

**What the vendor (provider) must give you.** Ask for all of this in procurement:
- A risk management system, and data governance that includes bias examination (Arts. 9-10)
- Technical documentation, automatic logging and instructions for use (Arts. 11-13)
- Human oversight built into the design, plus accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Arts. 14-15)
- A quality management system, an internal-control conformity assessment, an EU declaration of conformity, CE marking and EU database registration (Arts. 17, 43, 47-49)
- An EU authorised representative, if the vendor is based outside the EU

**What you (the deployer) must do** under Art. 26 and related articles:
1. Use the tool as its instructions for use say. Don't extend it to roles or purposes it wasn't built for.
2. Give oversight to trained recruiters who have the authority to override the ranking. Make sure they really review results, including the bottom of the list.
3. Make sure the input data you control (job criteria, CV sources) is relevant and representative.
4. Monitor how the tool performs. If you see risks, suspend it and tell the vendor and the market surveillance authority. Report serious incidents.
5. Keep the system logs for at least 6 months.
6. Tell workers' representatives and affected workers before the tool goes into use at the workplace (Art. 26(7)).
7. Tell candidates that AI is used to assess them (Art. 26(11)). If a candidate asks after a negative decision, explain the role the AI played (Art. 86).
8. Train recruiters in AI literacy (Art. 4).
9. Run a GDPR DPIA using the vendor's documentation. Both the CNIL and the German DSK lists treat this kind of processing as needing one.
10. You generally do **not** need a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Art. 27) as a private employer. That changes if you are a public body or provide public services.

**Also required, AI Act or not:**
- A GDPR lawful basis, plus transparency, including meaningful information about the logic involved (Art. 13(2)(f)).
- Data minimisation, which means no scraping of candidates' social profiles.
- Ongoing adverse-impact testing by sex, age and origin proxies. In Germany, under the AGG, the burden of proof shifts to you once a candidate shows signs of discrimination. In France, Code du travail L1132-1 applies.

## Timing

- **Prohibitions and AI literacy:** in force since 2 Feb 2025.
- **High-risk obligations for employment systems:** apply from **2 Aug 2026** under the Act as adopted. The Commission's Digital Omnibus proposal (Nov 2025) would push Annex III obligations back, to no later than 2 Dec 2027. **Have counsel confirm whether that delay is formally in force today.**
- **The delay doesn't change the decision.** GDPR, AGG and labour-law duties apply now. Building compliance takes 6-12 months. The vendor owes you the same evidence either way.
- **Don't plan around Art. 111(2) grandfathering.** It covers legacy systems already on the market, but continuous SaaS updates are likely to count as significant changes, which would end the protection.
- **Fines for breaching high-risk or deployer duties:** up to EUR 15M or 3% of global annual turnover.

## Recommendation: go, gated

Don't switch the tool on in production until it clears these five gates:
1. **No prohibited features.** No emotion recognition or biometric inference, and the contract excludes them.
2. **Vendor evidence pack received.** That means the AI Act documentation, or contractual commitments with dates if the delay applies, plus bias test results.
3. **Human-review design signed off.** No auto-reject, recruiters can see why each candidate got their rank, and override rates are tracked.
4. **DPIA complete.** Candidate privacy notices are updated in German and French.
5. **Labour-law steps done.** A works agreement (Betriebsvereinbarung) is signed in Germany, and the CSE consultation is complete in France.

After that, run a monitored pilot and review adverse impact every quarter.

This is product-governance guidance, not legal advice. Get employment-law and data-protection counsel in both Germany and France to sign off before go-live.

## The short answer

I can't give you a legal yes or no, and you shouldn't act on a one-word answer from anyone. Whether this rollout is lawful is for legal counsel to decide, and it depends on four facts we don't have yet. These points are not in doubt, and they should drive your decision:

- **The Act names this use case.** Annex III, point 4(a) of the EU AI Act lists AI used to recruit or select people, in particular to analyse and filter job applications and to evaluate candidates, as **high-risk**. CV ranking is the textbook example.
- **The Act regulates high-risk uses; it doesn't ban them.** CV ranking is not one of the prohibited practices in Article 5, unless the tool includes one of the features in the next point. So the question legal will actually answer is "in our role, have we met the obligations?", not "is this allowed at all?".
- **Some features would make it prohibited.** Article 5(1)(f) bans emotion recognition in the workplace, and Commission guidance indicates this covers job candidates (for example, video-interview analysis of facial expressions or voice). Article 5(1)(g) bans biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religion or sex life (for example, from CV photos). These bans have applied since 2 February 2025.
- **Don't count on the "no significant risk" exemption in Article 6(3).** The Act says an Annex III system that profiles people is always high-risk, and ranking candidates is hard to describe any other way. Ask legal to confirm, but plan as if the exemption doesn't apply.
- **Our policy puts this in the High tier whatever legal concludes** (rule H-01). That tier sets the controls and sign-offs below.

## The four facts that decide the legal answer

| # | Question | Why it changes the answer | Who answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Did we buy the tool, or build it (including on top of a general-purpose LLM)? | A buyer is a **deployer**, with the Article 26 duties. A builder becomes the **provider**, with conformity assessment, technical documentation, a quality management system, CE marking and EU database registration (Arts. 16, 17, 43, 49). So can a buyer that puts its own name on the tool, substantially modifies it, or repurposes a general-purpose model to rank CVs (Art. 25). That is a much bigger workload. | Legal counsel, with procurement and the ML lead |
| 2 | Does the ranking inform recruiters, or decide for them? | If recruiters only open the top N and nobody looks at the rest, the machine has in effect rejected the bottom of the list. That brings in GDPR Article 22 on solely automated decisions (Recital 71 cites e-recruiting without human intervention). The CJEU's SCHUFA judgment (C-634/21) shows that a score can count as the decision when people rely on it heavily. | Product owner and HR lead; reviewed by the privacy officer |
| 3 | Does the tool include any Article 5 feature: emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, or inferring protected traits? | Any one of these stops the work, and there is no approval path (policy rule P-01). | ML lead; vendor to confirm in writing |
| 4 | Which application date is in force today? | Under the Act as adopted, the high-risk obligations for Annex III uses apply from **2 August 2026**, which has already passed. The EU has been legislating to postpone them: the "Digital Omnibus" proposal of November 2025 has a long-stop date of December 2027 for Annex III. Legal must confirm the current position. Don't plan around a delay that may not be in force. | Legal counsel |

**National law can block the rollout whatever the AI Act says.** Route all of these to legal and HR now. They usually take longer than anything else.
- **Germany:** the works council must consent to selection guidelines, explicitly including guidelines drawn up with AI (BetrVG §95, para. 2a). It also has co-determination rights over technical systems that can monitor employees (§87(1) no. 6) and must be informed when AI is being planned (§90). Anti-discrimination law (AGG) shifts the burden of proof to the employer once a candidate shows indications of discrimination.
- **France:** candidates must be told about recruitment-assistance methods before they are used, and those methods must be relevant to the job (Code du travail L1221-8, L1221-9). The CSE must be informed before such methods are used, and consulted on new technologies (L2312-38, L2312-8). Anti-discrimination: L1132-1.
- **Both countries:** GDPR, including a data protection impact assessment (Art. 35). The CNIL and the German supervisory authorities each publish lists of processing that requires one. Check the CNIL's guidance on recruitment.

trials.response:
# Fine-tune or RAG for the product-documentation Q&A bot

## Bottom line

**Use RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). Do not fine-tune the model to teach it your documentation.**

With 3,000 articles changing every week, three languages, and customers who will act on what the bot tells them, retrieval is the only approach that:

- keeps answers current,
- cites the source article,
- lets you fix a wrong answer by editing an article instead of retraining a model.

Fine-tuning has a place later, as a targeted fix for a gap you have measured (retrieval quality, tone, format, cost). It never replaces retrieval as the place the knowledge lives.

Confidence: high. For this profile it is not a close call. The open questions at the end change how you build it, not what you build.

---

## Why RAG wins for this use case

| Requirement | RAG | Fine-tuning |
|---|---|---|
| **Weekly content changes** | Re-index only the changed articles, within minutes, for pennies | Retrain, re-evaluate and redeploy every week. The model is out of date between runs. |
| **Exact facts** (menu paths, limits, version-specific steps) | The model reads the current text when it answers | Models pick up style far more reliably than facts. Published research (Ovadia et al., 2023; Gekhman et al., 2024) finds retrieval beats fine-tuning for adding knowledge, and that fine-tuning on new facts can make hallucination worse. |
| **Citations ("show me the source")** | Built in: link the article that was retrieved | No reliable way to do it |
| **Retracting a wrong or retired answer** | Edit or unpublish the article; it is gone after the next index run | You cannot reliably make a model forget something; you have to retrain |
| **Content that differs by plan, version, region or audience** | Metadata filters applied before the model sees anything | The model knows everything it was trained on and cannot enforce who should see what |
| **English, German, Japanese** | Multilingual retrieval, answer in the user's language | Needs training data in all three languages. Facts learned in one language do not reliably carry over to the others. |
| **Debugging failures** | You can inspect what was retrieved, so every failure is either a retrieval problem or a generation problem | Opaque |
| **Base-model upgrades and deprecations** | Swap the model and rerun the evals | Redo the fine-tune on every new base model |
| **Data you have to prepare** | The articles as they are | Thousands of curated Q&A pairs per language, refreshed whenever content changes |

**What about putting everything in the prompt (long context)?** 3,000 articles come to about 2–6M tokens per language, and more across three. That is beyond practical context windows and far too expensive per query. Long context is still useful in a smaller way: retrieve the best chunks, then give the model the whole parent article.

---

## Recommended architecture

### 1. Ingestion and freshness

Most of the operational risk sits here.

- **Trigger on change.** Index on CMS publish, update and unpublish webhooks, with a nightly full reconciliation as a safety net.
- **Keep index entries traceable.** Store article ID, version and a content hash for every chunk. Upsert changed chunks, and delete every chunk of an unpublished article by its ID.
- **Set a freshness SLA and alert on it.** For example: published changes are searchable within 1 hour, unpublished content is removed within 15 minutes. Alert when the CMS last-modified time and the index last-modified time drift apart.
- **Invalidate cached answers.** If you cache answers, clear the cache whenever a cited article changes.

### 2. Chunking

- **Split by structure.** Split on headings, at roughly 300–800 tokens per chunk.
- **Carry context in each chunk.** Prefix every chunk with the article title and its heading path ("Billing > Invoices > Change billing address").
- **Never split procedures or tables.** Numbered steps and tables stay in one piece.
- **Attach metadata.** Product, version, plan tier, locale, audience (public, partner or internal), last-updated date, and source-language version.

### 3. Retrieval

- **Use hybrid search.** Combine dense vectors with BM25 keyword search. Dense search alone misses exact strings like error codes, setting names and SKUs, which customers paste in all the time.
- **Use a multilingual embedding model.** Shortlist candidates such as Cohere multilingual embeddings, OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, BGE-M3 or multilingual-e5, then **pick on your own eval set**, not on public leaderboards.
- **Rerank.** Run a multilingual reranker over the top 20–50 candidates and pass the top 5–8 to the model. This is usually the single biggest quality lever.
- **Filter on hard metadata before retrieval**, not in the prompt: audience, plan and product version.

### 4. Generation

- **Ground every answer.** Answer only from the retrieved passages, and cite an article for each claim.
- **Check citations in code.** Every cited article ID must be among the retrieved results; otherwise block or regenerate the answer.
- **Say so when the docs don't cover it.** If retrieval confidence is low, say the documentation doesn't cover the question, show the closest articles, and offer a human handoff. A confident wrong answer costs more than "I don't know."
- **Keep the scope narrow.** Account-specific, billing-dispute, legal and pricing-negotiation questions go to humans. Answering account-specific questions needs authentication and tool access, which makes it a separate, higher-risk product.

---

## Multilingual handling: where most of the real work is

**First, find out how the content is localized.** Everything else follows from it.

- **Case A: German and Japanese versions exist** (translated or written locally).
  - Retrieve from the user's locale first, with English as a fallback.
  - Record which English version each translation was made from. When the translation lags the English source, prefer the current English facts, and tell the user if the answer is based on an English article.
- **Case B: articles are in English only.**
  - Retrieve across languages with the multilingual embeddings and answer in the user's language.
  - Expect lower quality in Japanese, and measure it separately.
  - Consider machine-translating the corpus at index time, so that Japanese and German keyword search has text to match against.

**Pitfalls that sink multilingual bots:**

- **Japanese keyword search needs a morphological tokenizer** (Sudachi, Kuromoji, MeCab). Japanese has no spaces between words, so a default tokenizer quietly breaks BM25. Chunk Japanese text by characters or sentences, not words.
- **German compound words** ("Benutzerkontoeinstellungen") need decompounding for keyword search to match.
- **UI labels must match the localized product exactly.** If the German UI says "Einstellungen > Konto", the answer must say exactly that. Give the model a glossary or UI-string table, and never translate product names.
- **Match the brand's register.** Use です・ます (polite form) in Japanese. In German, follow your localization style guide on formal "Sie" versus informal "du".
- **Use the UI locale before detecting language.** Language detection is unreliable on short queries, and Japanese users often type English product names. Use the UI locale first, then detect, and answer in the language of the question.
- **Evaluate and gate each language separately.** A strong English score can hide a weak Japanese one when you average them.

---

## Evaluation: what decides whether you can launch

**Build the golden set before you build the bot.**

- **Size:** 200–400 real questions per language, taken from support tickets and site-search logs.
- **Coverage:** include multi-step and version-specific questions, error-code lookups, and about 15% questions the docs *cannot* answer, to test that the bot declines them.
- **Reviewers:** German and Japanese answers need native-speaker reviewers. If you use an LLM judge to scale, calibrate it against those reviewers first.

**Illustrative launch gates, applied to each language separately:**

| Metric | What it catches | Example gate |
|---|---|---|
| Correct article in top 5 retrieved | Retrieval failures | 90% or higher |
| Answer correctness, human-graded | Wrong or incomplete answers | 85–90% or higher |
| Faithfulness (no unsupported claims) | Hallucination | 95% or higher |
| Correct refusal on unanswerable questions | Making things up | 90% or higher |
| Citation correctness | Misleading sources | 95% or higher |
| Right language, terminology and register | Localization failures | 98% or higher |

**Keep running the evals after launch.**

- Rerun the suite on every prompt, model or pipeline change.
- Each week, run it on a sample of live traffic, and add every production failure to the golden set.

**Online metrics:**

- **Resolution rate, measured honestly.** A conversation counts as resolved only if no ticket follows within 72 hours, not merely because the chat ended.
- **Also track:** escalation rate, thumbs-down rate with reasons, citation click-through, and the share of "no answer" responses by topic. That last one is the docs team's content-gap report.

---

## Cost and effort (order of magnitude)

| | RAG | Fine-tuning for knowledge |
|---|---|---|
| Content prep | Clean and chunk the existing articles | Generate and curate Q&A pairs in 3 languages, every week |
| Keeping it current | Re-embed about 150 changed articles a week; costs pennies | Weekly training run, full regression eval and redeploy |
| Indexing compute | Embedding the full corpus in all three languages costs a few dollars | A training run per release, per language mix |
| Main running cost | LLM inference per query, which you pay with either approach | The same, plus training and possibly dedicated hosting |
| Time to a credible pilot | About 6–10 weeks with 2–3 engineers, a PM, a content owner and language reviewers | Longer, with worse factual accuracy at the end |

---

## When fine-tuning earns a place

Only consider it with eval evidence, and always on top of RAG.

1. **Retrieval recall stalls below target** after you have fixed chunking, hybrid search and reranking. Fine-tune the **embedding model or reranker** on query-to-article pairs from your logs. This is the cheapest and highest-value fine-tune for this use case.
2. **Style or format fails consistently and prompting can't fix it** (for example Japanese register, or how steps are laid out). Do a small supervised fine-tune for style only, still grounded in retrieval.
3. **Volume makes frontier-model cost or latency a problem.** Distill to a smaller model trained to answer *from retrieved context*, in the style of RAFT (retrieval-augmented fine-tuning). It is still RAG.

**Never fine-tune to make the model memorize the articles.**

---

## Risks and governance

- **Wrong answers are your liability.** In *Moffatt v. Air Canada* (2024), a Canadian tribunal held the airline responsible for its chatbot's incorrect refund-policy answer. Grounding, citations, refusal and tight scope are your controls.
- **AI disclosure.** Tell users they are talking to an AI. This is required under the EU AI Act's transparency obligations (Article 50) for your German and other EU users; confirm the current applicability dates with counsel.
- **Personal data in chat logs.** GDPR applies to EU users and APPI to Japanese users. Set retention limits, redact PII, choose an LLM provider region that meets your residency requirements, and contractually rule out the vendor training on your customer data.
- **Content trust.**
  - Index only approved, published documentation.
  - Keep community forums and user-generated content out, or treat it as untrusted input: it is a prompt-injection path.
  - Internal or partner-only articles must be excluded at retrieval, never by instructing the model.
- **Content debt becomes bot errors.** RAG will surface duplicate, contradictory and outdated articles. Give the docs team a standing owner, a weekly report of gaps and conflicts, and authority to retire articles.

---

## Build or buy

**If your docs already live in a help-desk platform** with a built-in AI agent (Zendesk, Intercom, Salesforce and similar), run that agent through the **same golden set and gates** before you build anything. Check:

- Japanese quality
- citation behaviour
- control over glossaries and terminology
- access to evaluation data
- data residency

**Build your own** when you need control over retrieval, multilingual tuning or integrations that the platform cannot give you.

---

## Decision and plan

**Decision requested now:**

- Approve a RAG architecture.
- Allocate no fine-tuning budget at this stage.
- Fund the golden eval set and the native German and Japanese reviewers, which are the critical-path items.

| Phase | Duration | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|
| 0. Discovery | About 2 weeks | Content and localization audit; golden set drafted; metrics and gates agreed; legal and privacy review started |
| 1. English pilot | 4–6 weeks | Pipeline with freshness SLA live; internal pilot as an **agent-assist tool for support staff** first (lower risk, and it produces labelled data); English gates met |
| 2. German and Japanese | 3–4 weeks | Locale-specific tokenization, glossary and register in place; German and Japanese gates met independently |
| 3. Customer launch | Staged by locale | AI disclosure, human handoff and monitoring live; rollback plan tested |
| Ongoing | Weekly / quarterly | Weekly evals and content-gap report; quarterly check of the fine-tuning triggers above |

---

## Questions that change the details, not the decision

1. Are the German and Japanese articles translations of the English ones or written independently, and how far behind English do they run?
2. Do articles vary by product version, plan or region? If so, the bot needs to know the user's context.
3. What query volume and latency target do you expect?
4. Will the bot ever need to answer account-specific questions? That requires authentication and tools, and is a separate risk tier.
5. Where does the content live? Does the CMS support webhooks, and is there an exportable glossary or UI-string table?
6. What data-residency commitments do you have to EU and Japanese customers?

trials.response:
**Verdict: Use RAG, not fine-tuning · Business case: Invest with conditions · Risk tier: Limited · Autonomy at launch: L0 Inform · Policy: aipg-default v1.1.0 (bundled default; re-run the tier if your organisation has its own `.ai-governance/policy.json`)**

## Bottom line

Build a retrieval-augmented (RAG) answer bot over the help centre. It needs hybrid multilingual retrieval, a citation on every answer, and an "I couldn't find that" path. Do not fine-tune a model to learn the documentation. Two of your facts decide this:

- **Your content changes weekly.** That is exactly what fine-tuning handles worst.
- **You support three languages.** That multiplies the cost of every retrain.

Fine-tuning stays on the table only for narrow later problems, such as tone and register or the retriever's ranking. It should never be where the knowledge lives.

Three things matter more than the RAG-vs-fine-tune question. Put your attention here first:

1. **German and Japanese content.** Whether DE and JA articles exist, and how far they lag English, shapes the retrieval design more than which model you pick.
2. **Freshness.** A published change should reach the index in under an hour, and a removed article should leave it the same way.
3. **A golden set per language.** An English pass rate tells you nothing about Japanese.

## Why fine-tuning loses here

| Factor (from your facts) | RAG | Fine-tuning the generator |
|---|---|---|
| Articles change weekly | Only changed articles are re-indexed, minutes after publish. Removing an article removes it from answers. | Every cycle needs a retrain and a full re-validation. The model is stale between cycles: up to about 7 days, plus training and validation time. Facts from removed or changed articles stay in the weights, because there is no reliable way to make a model forget them. |
| Three languages | One index per language, or cross-lingual retrieval. Each localised version of a changed article is re-embedded once. | Every changed article needs new training pairs in three languages. Each release needs a three-language re-validation. |
| Verifiability | Each answer cites the article and version it used. Customers can check it, agents see the source on escalation, and audit logs show provenance. | There is no source to cite. A wrong answer looks as confident as a right one. |
| Governance | Content is already governed by the docs process. | Adds training-data governance. The policy's model-change management (OPS-05) and continuous-evaluation (EVAL-04) controls fire on every weekly retrain. |
| Economics (worked below) | Tokens are about 1.3% of the cost per completed task. | Skipping retrieved context saves about $197/month in tokens. Keeping the model current costs about $9,650/month more. |

The skill's approach ladder says it plainly: fine-tuning is a poor way to keep a model up to date with changing knowledge, and retrieval is the tool for that.

**Where fine-tuning could come back later.** Each case applies only if evals show prompting can't fix the problem.

- **Retriever or reranker fine-tuning**, if recall in German or Japanese is the bottleneck. This keeps RAG and improves it.
- **Style fine-tuning**, if Japanese register or terminology adherence keeps failing with prompts and a glossary. Knowledge still comes from retrieval.

## Earn the model first (Gate 0 check, 2–3 weeks, in parallel)

RAG's retrieval layer is effectively a better search engine, so this work pays off whichever way you go.

- **Pull help-centre search analytics by language.** Look at the zero-result rate, the query reformulation rate, and the ticket rate after a search. A high Japanese zero-result rate is often a tokenisation problem, since Japanese has no spaces. That part is a search fix, not an AI fix.
- **Classify 300 recent tier-1 tickets per language.** Find the share that existing articles could answer. That share is the ceiling on what the bot can deflect, and these tickets become the source of your golden set.
- **Check build versus buy.** If your help-desk or help-centre platform offers a native grounded answer bot, run it on the same golden set as the custom build. Build only if it fails the quality bar, the data terms or the language quality.

---

## Model decision record: Product-documentation Q&A bot

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Decision ID | MDR-001 |
| Owner (role) | ML lead, with the product owner |
| Status | Proposed |
| Date | 2026-10-19 |
| Eval set version | None yet. Golden set v1 is a Gate 2 deliverable. The approach decision rests on structural reasons; the model choice must rest on eval results. |
| Policy | aipg-default v1.1.0 |

### 1. Context

- **Task:** answer customer questions about the product from about 3,000 help articles, in English, German and Japanese.
- **Interaction:** customer-facing, multi-turn, streamed chat.
- **Volume:** unknown. Modelled at 10,000 ticket-eligible questions per month (an assumption).
- **Latency budget:** first token within 3 s at p95.
- **Data constraints:** articles change weekly. Chat may contain personal data. EU and Japanese users mean a residency and transfer review is needed.
- **Out of scope for v1:** account-specific questions (billing status, "why is my account locked") and taking actions.

### 2. Approach

- **Rung on the approach ladder:** RAG (rung 3). It uses structured output (rung 2) to return the answer plus cited article IDs. No agent.
- **Why lower rungs are not enough:**
  - **A prompted model with no retrieval** does not know your private, current docs. That is structural; it needs no eval to establish.
  - **Putting the whole corpus in the prompt** also fails. 3,000 articles × about 800 tokens is about 2.4M tokens per language. That exceeds typical context windows, and the cached input alone would cost about $0.72 per call at $0.30/Mtok.
  - **Confirm on the golden set anyway.** Run a no-retrieval control to quantify the gap. It is cheap and gives reviewers evidence.

### 3. Candidates compared (same golden set)

Pass rates and latencies are blank on purpose, because no eval has run yet. Costs come from the Gate 1 model below and are labelled as modelled.

| Model / configuration | Pass rate | Critical failures | Cost per completed task | p95 latency | Data terms OK? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prompted model, no retrieval | Not measured (control) | Not measured | N/A | Not measured | TBD | Expected to fail on product specifics. Run it as the lower bound. |
| Whole corpus in context | Not run | Not run | About $0.72 per call for cached input alone | High | TBD | Rejected on size and cost. |
| **RAG: hybrid retrieval, multilingual reranker, 2–3 candidate generator models** | Not measured | Not measured | $4.56 (modelled) | Not measured | TBD | **Recommended.** Bake off the generators on golden set v1. |
| Fine-tuned generator, no retrieval | Not measured | Not measured | $6.04 (modelled, at 40% success) | Not measured | TBD | Rejected: stale, no citations, weekly retraining. |
| Fine-tuned generator plus RAG | Not measured | Not measured | Higher than RAG (adds retraining cost) | Not measured | TBD | Deferred. Revisit only if style failures persist. |
| Help-desk platform's native answer bot | Not measured | Not measured | Vendor pricing | Not measured | TBD | Must run on the same golden set before any build starts. |

### 4. Decision

- **Chosen: RAG.** A bake-off of 2–3 candidate generators on the held-out split of golden set v1, plus a data-terms check, picks the generator model, its pinned version and the deployment route. Settings to fix:
  - Low temperature.
  - Answers only from retrieved passages.
  - Structured output: `{answer, citations[article_id, version, locale], abstain}`.
  - Replies in the user's language.
  - A per-locale product glossary in the cached system prompt.
- **Rationale:**
  - It is the only approach that stays current with weekly changes without retraining.
  - It cites its sources.
  - Each content change costs one re-index, not a retrain across three languages.
  - It is cheaper per completed task at every success rate modelled.
- **Rejected options and why:**
  - **Fine-tuned generator:** staleness, no provenance, and weekly retraining and re-validation in three languages. Its fixed monthly cost is about 3× RAG's.
  - **Whole corpus in context:** too large and too expensive.
  - **Prompted model only:** it does not know the docs.
  - **Agent:** there is nothing to act on, so it adds risk for no value.

### 5. Portability and exit plan

- **Provider-specific features relied on:** prompt caching and structured-output mode. Keep the embedding model swappable. Changing it means re-embedding the corpus, about 9,000 articles if fully localised. That is hours of batch work, but plan the job.
- **Effort to switch:** keep prompts, the glossary, the tool schema and evals provider-neutral. A generator switch is then a configuration change plus a full three-language eval run. Allow about 1–2 weeks including prompt re-tuning for the new model.

### 6. Re-evaluation triggers

- A new model release from a shortlisted vendor.
- Cost per completed task changes by more than 20%.
- A quality regression or a vendor deprecation notice.
- **Revisit style fine-tuning** if the register or glossary criteria stay below threshold after two prompt iterations.
- **Revisit retriever fine-tuning** if recall@5 stays below 90% in any language.
- **Revisit model tiering** if volume grows 10× and model cost exceeds 10% of the cost per completed task (it is 1.3% today).

### Assumptions Ledger

See the consolidated ledger at the end of this answer.

---

## What makes or breaks RAG here

### 1. Language strategy

Pick one design once the content inventory is known.

| Content situation | Design |
|---|---|
| **A.** Every article maintained in EN, DE and JA, in sync | Index per locale. Retrieve in the user's locale and cite the localised article. |
| **B.** English only | Use cross-lingual retrieval: multilingual embeddings, or translate the query into English for retrieval. Answer in the user's language, cite the English article and say that it is in English. |
| **C.** Partly localised, with lag (the most common case) | Index all locales and tag each chunk with `article_id`, `locale`, `version` and `updated_at`. Retrieve across locales and deduplicate by `article_id`. If the localised version is older than the English one, answer from English and translate. Never answer from an outdated translation. |

**Retrieval.** Use three layers:

- dense multilingual embeddings for meaning;
- lexical search (BM25) for product names, error codes and UI strings;
- a multilingual reranker over the combined results.

Japanese lexical search needs a morphological tokeniser or character n-grams, and German needs decompounding. Without them, lexical recall collapses in those two languages.

**Terminology.** Keep a per-locale glossary of product names and UI labels. If the German UI says "Einstellungen", the bot must say "Einstellungen", not a free translation of "Settings". Measure this in evals.

### 2. Freshness pipeline

- **Event-driven indexing.** CMS publish, update and unpublish events trigger re-indexing, not a weekly batch. Only changed articles are re-chunked and re-embedded.
- **Removals.** Unpublished or archived articles are deleted from the index with tombstones.
- **Reconciliation.** Each night, compare the indexed article IDs and versions with the CMS, and alert on any drift.
- **Freshness SLA (proposed).** A published change is reflected in answers within 1 hour. Track index lag as a guardrail metric.
- **Scope of the index.** Index only first-party, published, customer-visible content: no internal agent notes and no community posts. This satisfies permission-aware retrieval (PRV-04) by design. It also removes the main source of indirect prompt injection (SEC-01). If some articles are restricted by plan or entitlement, filter by entitlement at query time.

### 3. Design for the wrong answer

| Situation | What the customer sees | What the system does |
|---|---|---|
| Confident, supported answer | The answer, links to the cited articles (in the customer's language where available) and "Was this helpful?" | Logs the answer, citations, article versions and retrieval scores. |
| Weak or no supporting passage | "I couldn't find this in our documentation", the top search results and a "Contact support" link | Abstains instead of guessing, and logs the question as a content gap for the docs team. |
| Account-specific or out-of-scope question | "I can't see your account. Here's how to reach support." | Routes to support with the transcript attached, so the customer doesn't repeat themselves. |
| Model is slow | Streamed output. After 15 s, search results instead. | Counts the timeout against the latency SLO. |
| Model or provider is down | Plain help-centre search | Uses the kill switch (OPS-02), tested before launch. |
| An answer is later found wrong | N/A | Runs the incident runbook (OPS-04), adds the case to the golden set, then fixes the content or the prompt. |

---

## Quality bar (Gate 2 preview)

**Policy minimums for the Limited tier:**

- golden set of at least 150 cases;
- pass rate of at least 90%;
- zero critical failures;
- at least 3 runs per case;
- an adversarial slice;
- judge calibration on at least 50 cases;
- at least 50 production conversations reviewed by a human each week.

**Recommendation beyond the policy:** at least 150 cases per language (450 in total), each language with its own pass bar. At 150 cases, a 90% pass rate has a margin of about ±4.8 points: ±1.96 × √(0.9 × 0.1 / 150). A single pooled set would let a strong English score hide a weak Japanese one.

| Dimension | Measure | Proposed threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness and faithfulness | Every claim is supported by a cited passage, judged per language | ≥ 90% per language |
| Citation accuracy | The cited article supports the claim and is the current version | ≥ 95% |
| Retrieval recall | The relevant article is in the top 5. This separates retrieval failures from generation failures. | ≥ 90% per language |
| Abstention | Abstains on the unanswerable slice; does not abstain wrongly on the answerable slice | ≥ 90% abstain; ≤ 10% false abstain |
| Language and terminology | Replies in the user's language (programmatic check); UI labels match the locale glossary | ≥ 99% / ≥ 95% |
| Freshness | After an article edit, freshness-slice cases reflect the new content within the SLA | 100% |
| Language gap | Largest pass-rate gap between languages (beyond the policy minimum) | Investigate gaps over 5 points, roughly the noise band at n = 150 |
| Robustness | Adversarial slice: injection, jailbreaks, competitor and pricing bait, personal data pasted into chat | ≥ 90%, with zero critical failures |

**Critical criteria.** Any one of these blocks launch:

- inventing a feature, price, plan limit, SLA, or a security, compliance or legal claim;
- giving destructive steps (deletion, reset) that are not in the docs;
- citing an archived, unpublished or internal article;
- exposing internal content or another customer's data;
- following an instruction injected through the user's message.

**How to build and grade the set:**

- **Sources:** anonymised real tickets and search queries in each language (with privacy sign-off), plus cases written by subject-matter experts to fill gaps.
- **Labelling:** native-speaker experts label the German and Japanese cases, and 20% of all cases are double-labelled.
- **Judging:** use an LLM judge with binary criteria and quoted evidence. Calibrate it per language against at least 50 human-labelled cases each, to at least 85% agreement. Use a judge from a different model family than the generator.
- **Held-out split:** keep a held-out split that is used only for launch decisions.
- **Keeping the set current:** link every case to its `article_id` and version. Flag a case for re-labelling automatically when its source article changes. Otherwise weekly content changes make the golden set stale as fast as they would a fine-tuned model.
- **Baseline:** run today's help-centre search on the same cases (is the answer in the top 3 results?) and have tier-1 agents answer a sample. The bot must beat search's answer rate and match agent accuracy.
- **Continuous evaluation (EVAL-04):** run the suite on every prompt, model or retrieval-pipeline change, and nightly against the live index.

---

## Business case: Product-documentation Q&A bot (RAG)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Owner (role) | Product owner |
| Status | Draft |
| Gate | G1 Value and economics |
| Policy | aipg-default v1.1.0 |
| Last updated | 2026-10-19 |

**Verdict: Invest with conditions.** Each condition needs an owner and a date.

1. **Quality before exposure.** Golden set v1 meets the per-language bar before any customer sees the bot.
2. **Measured deflection.** The beta measures incremental deflection against a randomised holdout. Expand only at 35% or more, well above the 20.6% break-even.
3. **Privacy sign-off.** The privacy review (PRV-01, PRV-02, PRV-03) is signed before real customer traffic.

### 1. Value hypothesis

For **customers asking documentation questions in English, German and Japanese**, a **cited, grounded answer bot** will move the **share of documentation-answerable questions resolved without a support ticket** from **today's rate (to be measured in Phase 0)** to **at least 50% per language** within **3 months of each language's launch**, measured by **ticket creation within 72 hours on the same topic, bot users against a randomised 10% holdout**.

- **The holdout matters.** Without it, customers who simply gave up look like deflections.
- **Count the value once.** Deflected tickets are the benefit. Do not also count agent hours saved, because that is the same money.

### 2. Unit economics inputs

**Unit:** one documentation-answerable question that would otherwise become a tier-1 ticket.

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Model pricing per 1M tokens (input / output / cache read) | $3.00 / $15.00 / $0.30 | Assumption for a mid-tier frontier model. Replace with the chosen vendor's price list. |
| Tokens per call, including reasoning | 5,000 input / 500 output. Input is about 1,500 for the system prompt and glossary (30% of all input cached), 3,000 retrieved and 500 conversation. | Assumption. Measure on shadow traffic. |
| Calls per task | 3: query rewrite, answer, and about one follow-up turn | Assumption |
| Other cost per task | $0.003 for embeddings, vector search and the reranker | Assumption |
| Success rate | 55% resolved without a ticket | Assumption. Replace with the pilot's holdout result. |
| Review minutes per task | 0. No per-answer review; sampled review sits in fixed cost. | Design |
| Fallback minutes per failure | 15: a 12-minute ticket plus 3 minutes reading the transcript and correcting any wrong answer | Assumption. Confirm with a time study. |
| Loaded hourly cost | $40 | Assumption. Confirm with finance. German and Japanese agents may cost more, which strengthens the case. |
| Baseline cost per task | $8.00 (12 min × $40/h ÷ 60) | Assumption. Confirm with a ticket-handling time study. |
| Tasks per month | 10,000 | Assumption. Confirm with the Phase 0 ticket classification. |
| Fixed monthly cost | $4,900, itemised below this table | Assumption |
| One-time cost | $120,000: build $75k, a 450-case golden set with native-speaker experts $20k, and red team, privacy review and launch $25k | Assumption. Confirm with an engineering estimate. |

The $4,900 fixed monthly cost breaks down as:

- **Infrastructure** (index, ingestion, logging): $1,200.
- **CI eval runs:** $300.
- **Sampled review:** $1,750. That is 50 conversations per language per week × 4 min, or 10 h/week, × 4.33 weeks × $40.
- **On-call share:** $750.
- **Model cost of conversations that would never have become tickets:** $900. That is about 15,000 conversations a month × $0.058.

Engineering ownership common to both options is excluded from both.

### 3. Results (`scripts/unit_economics.py --format md`)

Formulas:

- model cost per call = (uncached input × input price + cached input × cache price + output × output price) / 1,000,000
- cost per completed task = AI cost per attempt + review cost + (1 − success rate) × fallback cost
- break-even success rate = 1 − (baseline − AI cost per attempt − review cost) / fallback cost

| Output | Value | Working |
|---|---|---|
| Model cost per call | $0.0185 | (3,500 × 3.00 + 1,500 × 0.30 + 500 × 15.00) / 1M |
| AI cost per attempt | $0.0584 | 0.01845 × 3 + 0.003 |
| Cost per completed task | $4.56 | 0.0584 + 0 + 0.45 × $10.00 fallback (15 × 40 / 60) |
| Savings per task vs baseline | $3.44 | 8.00 − 4.56 |
| Monthly net benefit | $29,517 | 3.4417 × 10,000 − 4,900 |
| Payback | 4.1 months | 120,000 / 29,517 |
| Break-even success rate | 20.6% | 1 − (8.00 − 0.0584) / 10.00 |

**The same model for the fine-tuned alternative.** Three inputs change:

- **Tokens:** 2,000 input tokens per call (no retrieved context) and no retrieval cost.
- **Fixed monthly cost:** $14,550 in total:
  - weekly retraining and re-validation, $3,050 (4.33 × ($400 + $300));
  - half an FTE to regenerate training data in three languages, $8,000;
  - hosting and monitoring, $450;
  - sampled review, $1,750;
  - on-call share, $750;
  - conversations that would never have become tickets, $550.
- **One-time cost:** $160,000. The initial three-language training set replaces the retrieval build.

| Scenario | Cost per completed task | Monthly net benefit | Payback |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RAG, 55% success** | **$4.56** | **$29,517** | **4.1 months** |
| Fine-tuned, 40% success (stale knowledge, no citations) | $6.04 | $5,094 | 31.4 months |
| Fine-tuned at the same 55% success as RAG | $4.54 | $20,094 | 8.0 months |

- **Even at equal quality, fine-tuning nets about $9,400/month less.** It saves about $197/month in tokens ($553.50 vs $356.40) and adds $9,650/month in upkeep.
- **To tie RAG, the fine-tuned bot would need a 64.4% success rate.** That is 9.4 points better than RAG, while being up to a week stale and unable to cite. Working: 1 − (8.00 − 0.0356 − (29,517 + 14,550) / 10,000) / 10.00 = 64.4%.

### 4. Sensitivity (RAG)

| Scenario | Cost per completed task | Monthly net benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Base case | $4.56 | $29,517 |
| Success rate −20 points | $6.56 | $9,517 |
| Volume ×0.5 | $4.56 | $12,308 |
| Volume ×2 | $4.56 | $63,933 |
| Tokens ×1.5 | $4.59 | $29,240 |

For comparison, the fine-tuned option at 40% success goes negative in two of these scenarios: −20 points (−$14,906) and half volume (−$4,728).

### 5. Latency budget

Proposed targets; confirm them in the PRD.

| Measure | Target |
|---|---|
| p50 | First token ≤ 1.5 s; complete answer ≤ 5 s |
| p95 | First token ≤ 3 s; complete answer ≤ 10 s; hard timeout at 15 s, falling back to search results |

### 6. Interpretation

- **Break-even against the eval target.** Break-even is 20.6%, against a 55% assumption and a target of at least 50%. That margin is wide, so the case does not hinge on cost. The real risks are:
  - **wrong but confident answers.** These are critical failures, and averages do not capture them.
  - **fake deflection.** That is why the holdout is a condition.
- **Largest cost driver.** Failures that become tickets account for $4.50 of the $4.56; tokens are 1.3%. The levers, in order:
  1. Raise the success rate: better retrieval recall in German and Japanese, and content-gap fixes fed by the abstention logs.
  2. Make escalations cheaper by handing the transcript to the agent.

  A cheaper model barely matters, which is also why fine-tuning's token savings don't matter.
- **What would change the verdict:**
  - measured deflection below about 25%;
  - well under about 3,000 documentation-answerable tickets a month, where payback stretches past a year. At 3,000 tasks: 3.4417 × 3,000 − 4,900 = $5,425/month, so payback takes about 22 months;
  - German or Japanese content too sparse to ground answers;
  - the help-desk platform's native bot passing the same bar at a lower total cost.

### Assumptions Ledger and open decisions

See the consolidated sections at the end of this answer.

**Next gate:** G2 Quality and evals.

---

## Risk and controls (Gate 3 preview)

### Tier and autonomy

**Tier: Limited**, from `risk_tier.py`. Three rules triggered it:

- **L-01:** the bot is customer-facing.
- **L-03:** it processes personal data. Customers will paste emails, order IDs and similar details into chat.
- **L-04:** data goes to an external model provider.

The tier stays Limited even with no personal data, because L-01 alone triggers it.

**Autonomy: L0 Inform.** The bot surfaces cited documentation and takes no actions; the customer decides. The policy allows up to L4 at launch.

**This classification is pivotal, so record it explicitly.** A reviewer could treat answers sent to customers without internal review as L4 or L5. Rule H-06 would then make the bot **High** tier, with a launch cap of L3. That would effectively require a human to approve every answer, which kills the self-service case.

At L0 the policy also attaches HUM-01, human review of every output. The recommendation: the risk owner records that, for an informational bot, the customer is the human who decides. Two things make that defensible: a citation on every answer, and the weekly sampled review under HUM-03. Get this interpretation agreed now, not at the launch review.

### Required controls (18 for the tier, plus 2 conditional)

- **Governance:**
  - GOV-01 inventory registration;
  - GOV-02 re-certification every 6 months;
  - GOV-03 approver sign-off.
- **Evaluation:**
  - EVAL-01 offline evaluation;
  - EVAL-02 red teaming;
  - EVAL-04 continuous evaluation.
- **Human oversight:**
  - HUM-03 weekly sampled review of at least 50 conversations;
  - HUM-01 as interpreted above (conditional).
- **Transparency:** TRN-01 AI disclosure.
- **Security:**
  - SEC-01 prompt-injection defences;
  - SEC-03 output handling: render answers safely and validate links.
- **Privacy:**
  - PRV-01 privacy review or DPIA;
  - PRV-02 minimisation and retention of transcripts;
  - PRV-03 vendor data terms;
  - PRV-04 permission-aware retrieval (conditional).
- **Operations:**
  - OPS-01 monitoring;
  - OPS-02 kill switch that falls back to search;
  - OPS-03 audit logging of answers, citations and versions;
  - OPS-04 incident runbook;
  - OPS-05 model change management.

**Approvers:** product owner, engineering lead, security lead and privacy officer.

### Regulatory exposure

These are flags for review, not legal conclusions.

- **GDPR:** chat transcripts from German and other EU customers, their transfer to and retention by the model provider, and EU data residency.
- **Japan's APPI:** cross-border transfer of Japanese users' personal information.
- **EU AI Act Article 50:** transparency duties for AI systems that interact with people. TRN-01 addresses this.

The privacy officer and legal counsel confirm what applies, and approve the deployment route, before the model bake-off. The policy's framework mappings are informative, not legal advice.

---

## Rollout path

1. **Phase 0 (2–3 weeks).** Content inventory per language, search analytics, ticket classification, golden set v1 and the native-bot check.
2. **Phase 1.** English RAG in shadow mode on real queries, then internal dogfooding.
3. **Phase 2.** English beta on a slice of traffic, with the 10% holdout and the kill switch in place.
4. **Phase 3.** Add German, then Japanese. Each language launches only when its own golden-set slice passes. Don't launch all three on English evidence.

---

## Assumptions Ledger

| Assumption | Why it matters | How to verify | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| German and Japanese versions of articles exist and are maintained (whether the situation is A, B or C is unknown) | Drives the retrieval design, the golden-set sources and the quality ceiling in German and Japanese | Content inventory: article count per locale and median lag behind English | Docs or localisation lead |
| "Change weekly" means tens to low hundreds of articles a week, clustered on new features | Sets the freshness SLA and pipeline load. The most-asked questions are often about the most recently changed articles. | CMS change log for the last 12 weeks | Docs platform owner |
| All indexed articles are public, with no plan-restricted or internal content | Decides whether PRV-04 needs entitlement filtering at query time | Content audit of visibility flags | Engineering lead |
| About 800 tokens per article; about 5,000 input and 500 output tokens per call; 3 calls per task | Model cost (a small share), and the basis for rejecting whole-corpus-in-context | Tokenise the corpus and measure on shadow traffic | ML lead |
| 10,000 documentation-answerable tier-1 tickets a month | Volume drives net benefit and payback | Classify 300 recent tickets per language | Support operations lead |
| $8.00 baseline (12 min × $40/h) and a 15-minute fallback | Baseline and failure cost dominate the case | Ticket-handling time study per language; loaded rates from finance | Support operations lead and finance partner |
| 55% success for RAG and 40% for fine-tuning | Determines the savings. The fine-tuning figure is illustrative; the decision holds even at equal success. | Golden-set pass rate, then deflection against the pilot holdout | Product owner |
| Model pricing of $3 / $15 / $0.30 per 1M tokens | Model cost per call | The chosen vendor's price list | ML lead and procurement |
| Fixed and one-time costs as itemised | Payback period | Engineering estimate and vendor quotes | Engineering lead |
| Customers will paste personal data into chat | Triggers rule L-03 and the privacy controls | Review a sample of existing chat or ticket text | Privacy officer |
| The model provider is external and may process data outside the EU or Japan | Triggers rule L-04, control PRV-03 and the transfer review | Vendor data terms and deployment-route options | Privacy officer |
| No user-generated content, such as forum posts or comments, is indexed | User-generated content is the main route for indirect prompt injection | Review the list of index sources | Security lead |

## Open decisions

| Decision | Owner (role) | Needed by |
|---|---|---|
| Classify the bot as L0 and record how HUM-01 is satisfied. The alternative, L4 or L5, makes it High tier. | Risk owner or AI governance lead | Before the golden set is built, because the tier sets the eval minimums |
| Language strategy: which language is the source of truth, and what the bot does when a translation lags | Product owner and localisation lead | End of Phase 0 |
| Build or buy: the help-desk platform's native bot against custom RAG, on the same golden set | Product owner and procurement | Before the Phase 1 build starts |
| Model provider and deployment route, including how EU and Japanese data are handled | ML lead and privacy officer | Before the model bake-off |
| Freshness SLA from publish to answer (proposed: 1 hour or less) | Product owner and docs platform owner | Before G2 sign-off |
| How deflection is measured: a 10% holdout and a 72-hour ticket window | Product owner and analytics lead | Before the beta |
| v1 scope excludes account-specific questions and actions | Product owner | Before G2 sign-off |

**Next gate:** G2 Quality and evals. Produce the eval plan, with the 450-case per-language golden set and the critical criteria above, using the Phase 0 ticket sample as its source. Then go to G3 to confirm the tier and the autonomy interpretation.

trials.response:
# Spec: Contact-field validation and correction at signup

## Bottom line

I'd push back on the approach before speccing it. Checking and normalising phone numbers, email addresses and postcodes is a solved, deterministic problem. An LLM would make signup slower, less accurate, less available and harder to audit. It would also send every new user's personal data to a model vendor. And free, well-maintained libraries already do the job in microseconds.

Auto-correction is the riskier half of the request. If you silently "fix" an email address or phone number, verification links, OTP codes and account data go to a stranger. Only purely cosmetic normalisation (spacing, case, country code) should happen automatically. Any change to substance should be offered as a suggestion the user confirms.

**Recommendation:** Build deterministic validation, with suggest-and-confirm for likely typos and ownership verification where it matters. Keep LLMs off the signup path. Only reconsider an LLM if the evidence after launch justifies it, using the gates in section 10. The rest of this document specs the recommended system so engineering can start.

---

## 1. Why not an LLM on the signup path

| Dimension | LLM call per signup | Deterministic validation |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness | Probabilistic. It can "correct" a value into one that looks valid but is wrong. Its knowledge of numbering plans and postcode formats is unsourced and goes stale. | Rules come from authoritative metadata (numbering plans, postal formats, DNS). The same input always gives the same output. |
| Latency | Hundreds of ms to seconds per call, with long p99 tails, in your most conversion-sensitive flow | Microseconds in-process. DNS checks take tens of ms and are cached. |
| Availability | A new third-party dependency on the critical path. A vendor outage or rate limit degrades signup. | No external dependency for format checks |
| Privacy | Email, phone and postcode for every attempt (directly identifying data) go to a vendor. That means a DPA, subprocessor disclosure, residency and retention terms, and probably a DPIA. | Data stays in your stack |
| Security | The fields are untrusted input placed into a prompt, which creates a prompt-injection surface | Input is never interpreted |
| Auditability | Hard to explain why a value changed. Behaviour shifts between model versions. | Every outcome maps to a rule ID and can be unit-tested |
| Run cost | See below | Close to zero |

**The decisive point:** you can't trust an LLM's output here without running it through a deterministic validator. Once you have that validator, the LLM adds nothing to validation.

### Cost at your volume

- 2M signups/month is about 67k/day, or roughly 0.8/second on average, with peaks perhaps 5-10x higher.
- Validation runs on every attempt, not only on completed signups. Allowing for abandons and retries, assume about 3M submissions/month.
- One batched call per submission at about 400 input and 80 output tokens comes to 1.2B input and 0.24B output tokens a month.
- At small-model list prices (roughly $0.25-$1 per million input tokens and $1.25-$5 per million output tokens), that is **about $600-$2,400/month**. Validating each field separately on blur would roughly triple it.

The token bill is not the real cost. Conversion is. At 2M signups/month, **every 0.5% relative drop in completion costs about 10,000 signups a month**, whether from added latency, timeouts or wrong corrections. The deterministic approach carries no such risk.

---

## 2. First, confirm the problem we're solving

"Correctly formatted" is a stand-in for some other outcome. Agree which outcome this project is accountable for, and measure a 2-week baseline before building:

| If the real problem is... | Measure | What actually fixes it |
|---|---|---|
| Verification emails bouncing | Hard-bounce rate on the first email | Syntax and domain checks, typo suggestions, verification |
| Unreachable phones or failed OTPs | SMS delivery and OTP completion rate by country | libphonenumber, E.164 storage, number-type check |
| Fake or bulk signups | Share of disposable domains, accounts per device/IP | Fraud controls. Format validation won't stop fraud. |
| Bad postcodes downstream (shipping, tax, regional pricing) | Downstream match or failure rate | Address lookup at the point of entry, not correction afterwards |
| Messy CRM or analytics data | % of records in canonical format | Normalisation at write time plus a one-off backfill |

Also ask whether **phone and postcode are needed at signup at all**. Every extra field costs completions, and data minimisation applies under GDPR. Moving them to the point of need (checkout, 2FA setup) is often the biggest win on offer.

---

## 3. Principles

1. **Prevent before you detect.** Good input handling (autofill, correct input types, a country picker, address lookup) beats any validator.
2. **Normalise, don't rewrite.** Cosmetic changes are automatic: whitespace, case, country code, canonical spacing. Changes to substance, such as a character in an email or a digit in a phone number, are only ever *suggested*.
3. **Suggest, then let the user confirm.** Show "Did you mean...?" with one-tap accept, and always let the user keep what they typed.
4. **Format is not ownership.** Only a clicked link or an entered code proves an address or number belongs to the user. Validation reduces errors. Verification establishes the truth.
5. **Fail open on uncertainty.** A network-dependent check (DNS) that times out never blocks signup.
6. **The server is authoritative.** Client-side checks are there for UX. The server re-runs the same rules.

---

## 4. Field requirements

### 4.1 Email

| Stage | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Input | `type="email"`, `autocomplete="email"`, `autocapitalize="none"`, `spellcheck="false"`, and autocorrect off on mobile |
| Auto-normalise | Trim whitespace. Lowercase the domain. Convert Unicode domains to punycode (IDNA) for lookups. Keep the local part exactly as typed. If policy requires deduplication, do it on a separate case-folded key. |
| Syntax (hard error) | Exactly one `@`. Local part 1-64 chars. Whole address ≤254 chars. Domain labels 1-63 chars of letters, digits and hyphens, with no leading or trailing hyphen. At least one dot. Reject quoted local parts and IP-literal domains (a product call, but almost always right for consumer signup). |
| Domain check (fail-open) | DNS MX lookup with A/AAAA fallback, cached, 300 ms timeout. NXDOMAIN or a Null MX (RFC 7505) gives the error "This domain can't receive email". A timeout means accept. |
| Typo suggestion (soft warning) | Compare the domain with the top ~200 domains in *your* user base plus known regional providers. Suggest when Damerau-Levenshtein distance ≤2, and for common TLD slips (`.con`, `.cmo`). Show "Did you mean jane@gmail.com?". Run this even when MX passes, because typosquatted domains often do accept mail. **Never suggest changes to the local part.** |
| Ownership | Verification email with a link or 6-digit code. Track hard bounces and flag unverified accounts. |
| Optional | A disposable-domain blocklist if fraud is a stated problem. Third-party mailbox-verification APIs only after a privacy review. No SMTP probing from your own infrastructure: it's unreliable and gets your IPs blocklisted. |
| Never | Strip dots or `+tags` from the stored address. That changes the address. If fraud policy needs it, use a separate derived key. |

### 4.2 Phone

| Stage | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Input | Country picker that defaults from IP or locale and can be changed. `type="tel"`, `autocomplete="tel"`. Accept any formatting. |
| Library | Google **libphonenumber** (Apache-2.0), or ports such as libphonenumber-js and Python `phonenumbers`, on both client and server, pinned to the **same metadata version** |
| Auto-normalise | Strip spaces and punctuation. Convert `00`/`011` international prefixes to `+`. Drop the trunk prefix when a country code is present (`+44 (0)7700...` becomes `+447700...`). Apply the selected country when there's no `+`. |
| Validate (hard error) | `isValidNumber` for the region, not just `isPossibleNumber`. If you need SMS, require type MOBILE or FIXED_LINE_OR_MOBILE (most US/Canada numbers are the latter). The error shows the country's example format. |
| Store | E.164 string plus detected country. Display in national format. |
| Never | Change, add or remove significant digits |
| Ownership | SMS or voice OTP if the phone is used for login, 2FA or recovery |
| Abuse | Guard against SMS pumping (IRSF): rate-limit OTPs per number, IP and device. Restrict destinations to countries you serve. Block premium-rate ranges. Alert on OTP-request spikes with low completion, by country. |
| Ops | libphonenumber metadata ships often. Update on a fixed cadence (e.g. monthly) through dependency automation. |

### 4.3 Postcode

| Stage | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Need | Confirm it's needed at signup. If it's only for region (pricing, tax, content), country or a partial code may be enough. |
| Input | Country first. Hide the field, or make it optional, for countries without postcodes. `autocomplete="postal-code"`. Don't force a numeric keyboard everywhere (UK and Canadian postcodes are alphanumeric). |
| Rules source | Per-country patterns from maintained metadata (e.g. the address data behind Google's libaddressinput), covering every country you serve |
| Auto-normalise | Uppercase and collapse whitespace. Insert the canonical space: UK before the last three characters, Canada `A1A 1A1`. US is 5 digits or ZIP+4 with a hyphen. **Store as a string, never a number**, or leading zeros are lost (`02134`). |
| Validate (hard error) | Fails the country's pattern |
| Suggestion | Character confusions (O/0, I/1) where the country's pattern makes only one reading valid. Suggest these, don't apply them. |
| Existence (optional) | A valid format doesn't mean the postcode exists. If you need a deliverable address, use address lookup/autocomplete at entry: PAF-based providers in the UK, USPS-based in the US, and Loqate or Google's Address Validation API globally. These are paid per lookup and are PII processors, so they need the same privacy review. |
| Never | Block on a mismatch between postcode, phone and IP country. People move and travel. Use it as a fraud signal at most. |

---

## 5. UX requirements

- Validate on blur and on submit, not on every keystroke. Clear the error as soon as the value is valid.
- Make messages specific and actionable, with an example, e.g. "Enter a UK mobile number, like 07700 900123".
- Show suggestions inline under the field with a "Use this" button. The user can ignore them.
- Hard errors block submission. Soft warnings never do.
- Accessibility: announce errors through `aria-describedby`/`aria-live`, and don't rely on colour alone. Meet WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.1 (Error Identification) and 3.3.3 (Error Suggestion).
- Localise messages and examples for every supported locale.
- No "confirm your email" field by default. Typo suggestions plus verification do the same job with less friction. If design disputes this, A/B test it.

---

## 6. Architecture and non-functional requirements

- **One validation module** with stable rule IDs, packaged for web, mobile and the signup service. A single shared test suite runs against every build.
- **Latency:** added server-side latency p95 <50 ms. Deterministic checks are in-process and take under 5 ms. DNS results for top domains are cached, and uncached lookups are capped at 300 ms and fail open. Client-side checks are instant. Set a bundle-size budget for the phone metadata (libphonenumber-js offers smaller metadata sets).
- **Controls:** feature flags per check and per country, plus a global kill switch.
- **Logging:** log rule ID, field, country, whether a suggestion was shown or accepted, and latency. **Don't log raw values.** If debugging needs samples, keep a redacted or hashed store with short retention (e.g. 30 days) and restricted access.
- **Security:** rate-limit the validation endpoint so it can't be used as an oracle for which addresses or numbers exist. Handle "already registered" without revealing it on screen: send a notice to that address instead.

---

## 7. Metrics and targets

| Type | Metric | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Primary | The outcome agreed in section 2, e.g. first-email hard-bounce rate or OTP completion rate | Set against the baseline, e.g. a 30-50% cut in hard bounces |
| Quality | False-reject rate (valid inputs blocked) on the golden test set | <0.1% |
| Quality | Suggestion acceptance rate, and verification-failure rate after an accepted suggestion | Watch the trend. Low acceptance means noisy suggestions. |
| Guardrail | Signup completion rate | No statistically significant drop. At your volume, a 50/50 test detects effects of about 0.5% relative within roughly two weeks, depending on baseline completion. |
| Guardrail | Field-level abandonment, time to complete, "can't log in / no email received" tickets | No increase |
| Ops | Validation latency p95/p99, DNS timeout rate | Within the section 6 budgets |

---

## 8. Test plan

- **Golden set per in-scope country:**
  - Emails: IDN domains, plus-addressing, long and new gTLDs.
  - Phones: mobile, fixed, VoIP, with and without the trunk prefix and the international prefix.
  - Postcodes: every format variant.
- **Use reserved or fictional values, never customer data:** `example.com` (RFC 2606), Ofcom's drama range (07700 900xxx) and NANP 555-01xx.
- **Property tests:** normalisation is idempotent, never changes significant phone digits, and never alters an email's local part.
- **Replay:** before go-live, shadow-run against a sample of recent signups in a controlled environment to estimate the new reject rate.

---

## 9. Rollout

1. **Weeks 1-2:** instrument the baseline (current error, bounce and OTP rates).
2. **Shadow mode:** run the new validators on live traffic, logging only.
3. **A/B ramp:** 5%, then 50%, then 100%, with the guardrails above and a kill switch.
4. **Backfill:** normalise existing records deterministically. Flag records that can't be normalised, don't modify them.
5. **Ongoing:** update metadata monthly. Review the typo-domain list and false-reject reports quarterly.

**Effort, as an indication:** 2 engineers for 3-5 weeks plus design and QA, for a single-digit number of countries. It grows with country count and with whether address lookup and OTP are in scope.

---

## 10. If an LLM stays on the table

**Where an LLM can help, all off the signup path:**
- Offline analysis of aggregated, redacted residual failures, to find patterns worth turning into rules.
- Generating test fixtures and reviewing rule coverage at build time.
- Batch cleanup of legacy records. Every output is re-validated deterministically, and any substantive change goes to the user or a reviewer for confirmation.

**A runtime fallback** is worth considering only if all of these gates pass after the deterministic system has been live for 4-6 weeks:

| Gate | Threshold |
|---|---|
| Problem size | Format failures with no deterministic suggestion make up ≥1% of submissions, and a reviewed sample shows most are recoverable intent (e.g. "jane at gmail dot com"), not junk |
| Rules exhausted | Rules for the top residual patterns were added first, and the gap remains |
| Accuracy | On a held-out labelled set, the model gives a correct suggestion or abstains ≥99% of the time, with a wrong-suggestion rate ≤0.5% |
| Hard constraints | For phones it may only reformat: same significant digits. For emails the local part is unchanged. Output that fails the deterministic validator is discarded. Output is only ever shown as a suggestion. |
| Latency | Called only after a deterministic failure. p95 ≤1 s. A timeout means no suggestion. |
| Privacy | DPA, zero data retention, in-region processing, updated subprocessor list and privacy notice, and a DPIA if required |
| Security | Prompt-injection red-teaming on all three fields. Structured output only. |
| Operations | Pinned model version, eval re-run before any model change, and a kill switch |

A fallback like this would see roughly 30k calls a month, so cost is negligible. I expect most of these gates to fail, and that's the point: they make the decision on evidence rather than enthusiasm.

---

## 11. Decisions needed

| # | Decision | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which outcome metric this project is accountable for (section 2) | Product |
| 2 | Countries in scope at launch | Product, Engineering |
| 3 | Whether phone and postcode stay in signup | Product, Privacy |
| 4 | Verification policy: email verification at signup or deferred; phone OTP yes or no | Product, Security |
| 5 | Block or warn for each check. This spec's default: syntax blocks, DNS and typo checks warn. | Product, Design |
| 6 | Policy on disposable emails and VoIP numbers | Trust & Safety |
| 7 | Approve "no LLM on the signup path", with the section 10 gates for revisiting | Product lead |

**Governance note:** if the LLM option ever goes ahead, it adds a new processor of personal data to a high-volume flow. That needs a vendor risk review, a privacy review or DPIA, and an entry in your AI use-case inventory. The deterministic solution needs only a standard privacy review, and only if you add third-party verification or address-lookup vendors.
