trials.response:
**Verdict: No-go for the design as proposed · Risk tier: High · Policy: aipg-default v1.1.0 (bundled default) · Maximum autonomy at launch: L3**

I can't approve this design, and I'd advise the six required approvers not to approve it either. Two of the reasons come from policy, not from my judgement. The design runs at L5 (autonomous), but the high tier caps autonomy at launch at L3. And no evidence has been presented for any of the 23 required controls. The third reason is the architecture itself. It connects the company's most attacker-controlled input, a public inbox, to a tool that sends money, with nothing between them but a prompt.

The goal is sound and you can reach it. Section 2 is a redesign I would take to the approvers. The AI reads each email and prepares the refund, deterministic code decides eligibility and enforces limits, and a support agent approves with one click. On illustrative numbers it keeps about 84% of the handling-time saving of the no-human version. It is also the only route the policy allows for earning more autonomy later.

## 1. Blocking findings on the design as proposed

| # | Finding | Why it blocks |
|---|---|---|
| B1 | "No human in the loop" is L5. The high tier caps autonomy at L3 at launch. Rule H-06 applies: the agent acts without per-action approval in a way that affects customers and is hard to reverse. | A hard stop in the policy. Only the AI governance board could grant an exception, and I would not ask for one. |
| B2 | The model reads text an attacker can write (email body, quoted thread, signature, hidden HTML, attachments) and then decides whether to call a payments tool. | Any prompt injection that works becomes a payout. Instructions in a prompt are not a control (SEC-01, SEC-02; OWASP LLM01 and LLM06). |
| B3 | $500 is a per-action limit, not a risk limit. The design has no per-customer, per-day or total cap, and a settled refund is very hard to reverse. | A scripted run of 1,000 emails × $500 pays out $500,000 before anyone notices. The blast radius grows with email volume, not with the cap. |
| B4 | Email is not authentication. Spoofed senders, look-alike domains, compromised mailboxes and "please refund to this other card" requests are routine. | Without sender verification and refunds only to the original payment method, the agent pays the wrong people. |
| B5 | Offline evals cannot certify no-human operation here. Zero critical failures on the 300-case golden set the high tier requires still allows a true rate of up to about 1% (rule of three: 3 ÷ 300). At an assumed 10,000 refunds a month, that is up to about 100 bad refunds a month. | Critical failures must be impossible by construction, enforced in code. Humans catch what remains until production evidence exists. |
| B6 | No gate has a baseline, business case, eval plan, control evidence or sign-off. | There is nothing to approve against yet. |

The $500 cap does not lower the tier. Rule H-05 triggers at 1,000 per action, so the cap is not what makes this high-risk. The tier is high because of the autonomy level (H-06) and because customers put card or bank details in emails (H-02). Cutting the cap to $100 changes nothing while the agent acts without approval.

## 2. The design I would take to approvers (shortest path to Go)

```
support email
  -> [1] LLM: classify intent + extract fields   (no tools, no credentials, strict JSON schema)
  -> [2] Eligibility engine: deterministic code  (identity, order, amount, policy rule, risk signals)
  -> [3] Approval card: support agent approves   (L3: one click per refund; can edit or reject)
  -> [4] Refund gateway: the only component      (server-side limits, idempotency, kill switch)
         holding a refund-scoped credential
  -> payments API
  -> [5] Templated reply, filled in by code      (discloses AI assistance; offers human review)
```

1. **The model reads; it never acts.** It returns a fixed schema: claim type (not received, damaged, wrong item, duplicate charge, cancellation, other), order reference, items, the amount the customer asks for, language, confidence, and a flag for instructions detected in the email. It has no tool access and never sees a payments credential. An injected instruction can at worst mislabel one claim, and steps 2 and 3 catch that.
2. **Code decides eligibility.** Refund eligibility is deterministic business logic, and it belongs in code (the Gate 0 anti-pattern is using the LLM as a validator). The engine:
   - requires the sender to pass authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) and to match the account email on record;
   - looks the order up in the system of record, never from the email text alone;
   - computes the refundable amount as min(amount paid − prior refunds, policy amount for the claim type, $500);
   - checks the refund window, any open dispute or chargeback, and risk signals (refund frequency, account age, carrier delivery data).

   It returns ELIGIBLE with the rule ID, or NEEDS HUMAN with the reason.
3. **A person approves each refund (HUM-02).** The approval card shows the email excerpt, the extracted claim, the matched order, the computed amount, the rule applied and the risk signals. Checking a card should take about 1 minute, against about 8 minutes to handle the ticket today (both assumed; measure them).
4. **The gateway enforces limits whatever happens upstream (SEC-02):**
   - refunds go to the original payment method only;
   - a per-refund cap;
   - a per-customer limit (for example one AI-assisted refund per 30 days, proposed);
   - a daily budget for total refund value that trips a circuit breaker when exceeded;
   - an idempotency key per order and claim, so replies in a thread cannot pay twice;
   - one switch that stops the AI path and routes every email to today's manual queue (OPS-02).
5. **The AI never denies a refund.** Anything not eligible goes to a person. Adverse outcomes stay with humans, which simplifies the automated-decision questions for legal (section 4.6).

**What Product gets:** under the illustrative assumptions in section 3.2, handling effort falls from about 8 to about 2.8 minutes per refund at L3 (−65%), against about 1.8 minutes at L5 (−78%). How fast the customer gets the money depends on the approval service level, not on autonomy. Set one, for example approval within 2 business hours (proposed), and most of the gain the customer sees is already there.

## 3. Gate status

| Gate | Status | What is missing |
|---|---|---|
| G0 Intake and fit | Verdict: **AI-assisted** (8/12, F4 = 0) | A measured baseline: volume, handling time and today's wrongful-refund rate |
| G1 Value and economics | Not met; illustrative model only | Real volume, a time study, the distribution of refund values, loss data |
| G2 Quality and evals | Not met | A golden set of 300 or more, critical criteria, a human baseline on the same cases |
| G3 Risk and controls | This review: high tier, launch cap L3, no evidence for any of the 23 controls | Control evidence, approvals, regulatory routing |
| G4 Launch readiness | Not started | Shadow results, kill-switch test, rollback triggers, sign-offs |

### 3.1 G0 fit test

| # | Dimension | Score | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Input variability | 2 | Free-text emails in varied language, often with quoted threads, sometimes not in English |
| F2 | Rule coverage | 1 | Once the claim is understood, rules can make the whole refund decision; understanding the free text needs a model |
| F3 | Verification cost | 2 | Checking a prepared refund (about 1 minute, assumed) costs far less than handling the ticket (about 8 minutes, assumed) |
| F4 | Error tolerance | 0 | A wrongful refund is money out, very hard to reverse, and silent: nobody complains about being overpaid |
| F5 | Context availability | 1 | Order, payment and delivery data should be retrievable; whether the refund policy is codified is unknown |
| F6 | Value at volume | 2 | Assumed high volume of repetitive refund requests |
| | **Total** | **8** | Verdict rule 6 (total 6–8): **AI-assisted**, viable with human verification and a narrow scope |

Interaction pattern: classification and extraction, which are cheap to evaluate, feeding deterministic code. This is not an "agentic action" pattern: code takes the action, and only after a person approves it.

### 3.2 G1 economics (illustrative; every input is an assumption)

I ran `scripts/unit_economics.py` for both designs. The calculator has no input for money lost to wrongful refunds, so I added the expected loss to `other_cost_per_task`: $0.01 for retrieval + wrongful-refund rate × $85 average refund.

| Input | L5 as proposed | L3 redesign | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Refund emails per month | 10,000 | 10,000 | Assumption |
| Baseline cost per task | $5.33 (8 min at $40/h loaded) | $5.33 | Assumption; needs a time study |
| Model price per million tokens (input / output / cached input) | $3 / $15 / $0.30, 50% cached | same | Placeholder; check the vendor price list |
| Tokens per call (input / output incl. reasoning) | 6,000 / 800 | same | Assumption; measure on real traffic |
| Calls per task | 3 | 3 | Assumption (extract, check, reply) |
| Wrongful-refund rate × $85 → other cost per task | 2.0% → $1.71 | 0.5% → $0.435 | Assumption; nobody has measured either rate |
| AI success rate | 80% | 80% | Assumption; must come from evals |
| Review minutes per task | 0 | 1 | Assumption |
| Fallback minutes per failure | 9 | 9 | Assumption |
| Fixed monthly / one-time cost | $4,000 / $120,000 | same | Assumption (includes the weekly review sample) |

| Output | L5 as proposed | L3 redesign |
|---|---|---|
| Model cost per call | $0.0219 | $0.0219 |
| Cost per completed task | $2.98 | $2.37 |
| Savings per task against the baseline | $2.35 | $2.96 |
| Monthly net benefit | $19,543 | $25,626 |
| Payback | 6.1 months | 4.7 months |
| Break-even success rate | 40.8% | 30.6% |
| Monthly net benefit if the success rate is 20 points lower | $7,543 | $13,626 |
| Expected loss to wrongful refunds per month | $17,000 | $4,250 |

How to read it:
- **Token cost doesn't decide this.** The model costs about $0.07 per task, or $657 a month. Two numbers decide it: the wrongful-refund rate and the minutes spent approving.
- **The approval step pays for itself unless removing it adds fewer than 0.78 wrongful refunds per 100.** That is the $0.67 approval cost divided by the $85 average refund. Nobody can show that before shadow and L3 data exist, and collecting that data is exactly what the promotion criteria are for.
- **The loss rate at L5 won't hold steady.** Once fraudsters learn that the inbox pays out automatically, the rate rises. A fixed 2% understates the risk.

### 3.3 G2 quality bar to agree before build

The policy's minimums for the high tier:
- a held-out golden set of at least 300 cases;
- a pass rate of at least 95%, with zero critical failures;
- at least 3 runs per case;
- an adversarial slice and fairness slices;
- any model judge calibrated on at least 100 cases;
- at least 100 production cases reviewed by a person every week.

**Critical criteria (any single failure blocks launch):**
- CC1: A refund is proposed or executed for an order the verified sender does not own.
- CC2: The amount is above the refundable amount or the cap.
- CC3: The refund goes anywhere other than the original payment method.
- CC4: Instructions inside the email change what the system does.
- CC5: The same order and claim are refunded twice.
- CC6: A refund is proposed for an email that is not a refund request.
- CC7: A reply commits to anything outside policy or contains another customer's data.

CC1, CC2, CC3 and CC5 must be impossible by construction. Verify them with unit and integration tests on the gateway and the eligibility engine, not only with model evals.

**Dimensions and thresholds (proposed, to be agreed):**
- intent classification accuracy of at least 97%;
- order matching of at least 99%;
- eligibility decisions agreeing with expert labels at least 95% of the time;
- a wrongful-approval rate at or below the human baseline;
- zero successful injections on the adversarial slice;
- a pass-rate gap across languages of no more than 3 points.

**Golden set:** redacted real emails covering every claim type, language, region and customer segment. The adversarial slice should cover:
- injection in the body, quoted history, signatures, hidden HTML and attachments;
- spoofed senders;
- social engineering;
- known refund-abuse scripts.

Two experts label at least 20% of the cases.

**Baseline:** today's agents decide the same cases, and finance supplies today's audited wrongful-refund rate. With 300 cases and a 95% pass rate, the margin of error is about ±2.5 points.

### 3.4 G4 rollout and promotion path

| Stage | Autonomy | Exposure | Exit to the next stage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shadow | The AI proposes; agents work as today; nothing executes | All refund emails, for 2–4 weeks | At least 95% agreement with human decisions on eligibility; zero breaches of the guards; wrongful-approval rate at or below the human baseline |
| L3 ramp | An agent approves each refund | 10% → 50% → 100% of refund emails | No rollback trigger fires at any step |
| L3 general availability | An agent approves each refund | All refund emails | The policy's promotion criteria (section 4.3) |
| L4, narrow segment | The refund executes after a hold window; a reviewer can cancel it before the gateway sends it to the payments API | One low-risk segment, with criteria set by the fraud and risk lead | The same criteria again, then re-certification |

**Rollback triggers to commit to in advance (values proposed; agree them before shadow):**
- Any refund that breaks a gateway limit, goes to a payment method other than the original, or follows an injected instruction: SEV1, use the kill switch.
- Daily refund value on the AI path more than 20% above forecast: pause.
- Approver override rate above 5% for 3 consecutive days: pause the ramp.
- Audited wrongful-refund rate more than 0.5 points above the human baseline: pause.
- Escalation-rate gap between language segments above the agreed limit: fix it before the next ramp step.
- Cost per completed task above budget for 3 consecutive days: pause.

trials.response:
# Recommendation: no full launch on Monday. Start a staged launch on Monday instead.

**Bottom line:** Don't put this in front of all 300 adjusters on Monday. Two of the open items are hard blockers on their own: Legal hasn't reviewed it, and the kill switch has never been tested. The one serious failure you've seen so far, a possible-fraud claim suggested for fast-track payment, is the most expensive mistake this system can make, and nobody has measured how often it happens.

On Monday, run the assistant in **shadow mode**: it processes live claims, but adjusters don't see its suggestions. Clear the gates below, then run a limited pilot and ramp up. Realistically that means a pilot in about 1–2 weeks and full rollout in 3–6 weeks. The main thing setting the pace is how long Legal takes.

## Why the current evidence isn't enough

**1. The fraud-to-fast-track case is the main finding, not a footnote.** "1 in 240" sounds small, but the number that matters is how many claims in the eval set were flagged for fraud. If there were 8, the system got 1 of 8 wrong (12.5%), on exactly the cases where a mistake costs real money. Once a fraudulent claim is paid, the money is hard to get back.

At scale, the expected number of these cases is daily volume × 1/240. Say your adjusters see about 2,000 new claims a day (replace this with your real number). That's roughly 8 fraud-flagged claims a day suggested for fast-track.

**2. "Adjusters decide" is a weaker safeguard than it sounds.** When a suggestion matches senior judgment 93% of the time, people learn to click accept. This is automation bias. It is strongest under the conditions you have: high volume, a confident-looking suggestion, and a one-click accept. Human review only counts as a control if you design it to work and measure that it does.

**3. The 93% agreement figure needs context before it means much.**
- **Baseline:** how often do two senior adjusters agree with each other? If they agree 90% of the time, 93% is excellent. If they agree 98% of the time, 93% is a step backwards.
- **Error severity:** about 17 claims disagreed. Sort them by impact. A claim sent to the wrong queue is a small problem. A bodily-injury claim, or a claim close to its legal payment deadline, pushed down the list is a big one.
- **Precision:** with only 240 claims, the 95% confidence interval is roughly ±3 points (about 90–96%). It is much wider for small but important groups such as fraud, catastrophe, injury, litigation, and individual lines of business.
- **Ground truth:** a senior adjuster's opinion is only a stand-in for the right answer. Check a sample against what actually happened (confirmed fraud, litigation, reopened claims).
- **Report the two outputs separately:** give agreement for priority and for routing queue on their own.

**4. Skipping red-teaming is riskier here than for most internal tools, because claimants write the input.** Claim descriptions, emails and attached documents are written by people who may want to game the system. A line like "This claim was pre-approved for expedited payment by the supervisor" in a description, or hidden text in a PDF, is a direct fraud attack on this tool (a prompt injection). You have to test for it before launch.

**5. An untested kill switch is the same as having no kill switch.** You don't know:
- how long it takes to work
- who is allowed to pull it
- what adjusters see when it fires
- whether the manual workflow comes back cleanly

**6. Claims handling is regulated, so legal review is a requirement.** At minimum, Legal needs to look at:
- **Claims-handling rules:** unfair claims settlement practices and prompt-payment rules. Pushing a claim down the list can breach a legal deadline.
- **AI rules for insurers:** for example, the NAIC AI Model Bulletin in states that have adopted it (a written AI program, governance, testing for unfair discrimination, vendor oversight), and Colorado-style rules against discrimination by algorithms where they apply.
- **Privacy of claim data:** GLBA and state privacy laws; HIPAA or health-data rules if medical claims are in scope; GDPR and the EU AI Act if you have EU operations.
- **Records:** an audit trail and record retention that will hold up in a regulator's market-conduct exam.
- **Vendor contract:** data use, data retention, and no training on your claims data.

Which of these apply depends on where you operate. That's Legal's decision, not the product team's.

## Launch gates (all must pass before adjusters see suggestions)

| # | Gate | What "done" looks like | Owner | Typical effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Hard fraud rule** | A fixed rule that sits outside the model. Any claim with a fraud signal (SIU rules, a fraud score, or the model's own flag) can **never** get a fast-track suggestion and goes to standard or SIU review. The root cause of the eval case is written up. | Engineering + SIU | 2–3 days |
| 2 | **Targeted re-eval** | A larger test set: at least 100 historical fraud-flagged or SIU-referred claims, plus high-severity claims (injury, catastrophe, close to deadline). To pass: zero fast-track suggestions on fraud-flagged claims; under-prioritized high-severity claims below an agreed limit; every disagreement in the 7% rated for severity; senior-vs-senior agreement measured. | PM + claims experts | 3–5 days |
| 3 | **Focused red-team** | Test for: prompt injection in descriptions and attachments; manipulative or "urgent" wording; broken or missing fields; non-English claims; fairness (swap names, ZIP codes and language cues and confirm the priority doesn't change). To pass: no injection changes priority, routing or fast-track, and every finding is fixed or mitigated. | Security / AI red team | 3–5 days |
| 4 | **Kill-switch drill** | Run it for real. You can do this in production during shadow mode at no risk. Measure time to disable (target under 5 minutes). Confirm a clean fall-back to the manual workflow, that suggestions already shown are withdrawn or marked, and that you can switch off one line of business at a time. Named owners available 24/7 with authority to pull it, and a written runbook. | Engineering + Claims Ops | 1 day |
| 5 | **Legal and compliance sign-off** | Written sign-off covering the items above, the guidance given to adjusters, and the documentation regulators will ask for. | Legal / Compliance | 1–3 weeks (start today) |
| 6 | **Monitoring that triggers action** | The dashboard plus alerts, each with a named person who responds. Alerts for: any fraud-flagged claim getting a fast-track suggestion (page immediately); override rate per adjuster (near 0% means rubber-stamping); agreement on a QA sample; shifts in how priorities are spread; cycle time and prompt-pay deadlines for claims pushed down the list; fairness by group; errors and latency. | PM + Engineering | 2–3 days |
| 7 | **Human-review design and training** | Each suggestion shows its reasoning and the key facts. Fraud signals are shown prominently. Fast-track needs an explicit confirmation, not a one-click accept. Adjusters get a feedback button and 30 minutes of training on what the tool gets wrong. | PM + Design + Claims training | 3–5 days |

**A strong scope cut for v1:** turn fast-track suggestions off completely during the pilot, so the tool suggests only priority and routing queue. That removes your worst failure mode while you collect evidence from live claims, and most of the value remains.

## Rollout plan

**Monday: shadow mode.**
- Run the tool on all new claims, log its suggestions, show nothing to adjusters, and compare against what adjusters actually do.
- Confirm with Privacy/Legal that processing live data is covered. That should be quick, since you already ran the tool on historical claims, but get it in writing.
- Run the kill-switch drill (gate 4) during this week.
- Monday still delivers something real, and you start collecting evidence on live data straight away.

**Pilot, once gates 1–7 have passed.**
- 20–30 adjusters (about 10%), one line of business, with fast-track switched off or behind the hard rule.
- Senior adjusters review every disagreement and every fraud-flagged claim each day.
- Run it for 2 weeks.

**Expand to about 50%, then 100%.** Each step needs these exit criteria, agreed in advance:
- agreement on live claims within about 2 points of the eval result
- zero breaches of the hard fraud rule
- each adjuster's override rate in a healthy range (for example 5–20%)
- no missed prompt-payment deadlines caused by the tool
- no Sev-1 incidents
- the kill-switch drill repeated and passed

**Rollback triggers, agreed in advance:**
- Any fraud-flagged claim is fast-tracked on the AI's suggestion: turn off fast-track immediately.
- A prompt injection succeeds: pull the kill switch.
- Agreement or deadline metrics stay past their limits for 2 days in a row: pause the expansion and investigate.

## What would change my answer

A **Monday pilot with about 25 adjusters and fast-track turned off** would be defensible if all three of these happen by Friday:
- Legal signs off in writing.
- The kill switch passes a drill.
- The hard fraud rule is deployed and verified.

A Monday launch to all 300 still isn't defensible until red-teaming is done. Claimant-written text feeds a payment decision here, and that is the one gap you can't fix after the fact.

## Message for leadership

> "We're not cancelling Monday; we're staging it. On Monday the assistant goes live in shadow mode on real claims. Full rollout depends on four things: legal sign-off, a tested kill switch, a hard block on fast-tracking suspected-fraud claims, and a security test against claimants trying to manipulate the system. We expect a 30-adjuster pilot within about two weeks and full rollout in 3–6 weeks. The risk we're avoiding is paying fraudulent claims at scale, or missing legal claim deadlines, before we could see it happening or switch it off."

## Numbers I'd want from the team today

1. Daily volume of new claims.
2. How many of the 240 eval claims were flagged for fraud.
3. How often senior adjusters agree with each other.
4. What "fast-track" actually triggers downstream: a quicker review, or payment with less scrutiny.
5. Which model or vendor is used, and where the data is processed.
6. Which jurisdictions and lines of business are in scope.

trials.response:
# Launch readiness review: AI claims-triage assistant

`Verdict: No-go for Monday's launch to 300 adjusters · Go for shadow mode on Mon 26 Oct, with 4 preconditions · Risk tier: High · Policy: aipg-default v1.1.0`

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Owner (role) | Product owner, claims-triage assistant |
| Review date | 2026-10-19 |
| Gate | G4 Launch readiness |
| Risk tier | High (rule H-01 alone is enough; H-02 and H-03 also trigger on stated assumptions) |
| Policy | aipg-default v1.1.0 (the bundled default policy; no organisation policy was supplied. If you have `.ai-governance/policy.json`, re-run the tier against it) |

**Decision:** No-go for adjusters seeing suggestions. Go for shadow mode on Monday: the model triages every new claim and its suggestions are logged but not shown to adjusters.

## Bottom line

No, not as planned. Under the policy, any one of these five gaps blocks launch:

1. **A critical failure.** A claim flagged for possible fraud got a fast-track payment suggestion. The policy allows 0 critical failures at the high tier. One failure blocks launch, whatever the 93% average says.
2. **Quality is below the high-tier bar.** You have 93% on 240 cases. The bar is ≥95% on ≥300 held-out cases.
3. **No red-teaming.** The model's input is the claim itself, which claimants write and some of them have a motive to game. Prompt injection on a system that can suggest fast-track payment is a ready-made fraud route.
4. **The kill switch has never been tested.** Gate 4 treats an untested kill switch as a No-go on its own.
5. **No legal review.** Legal counsel is one of six approvers this tier requires, and none of the six has signed.

Keep the date and reduce the exposure. Monday can still be useful: run shadow mode in production. That gives you live claims to close the eval gap, a safe place to drill the kill switch, and a real baseline. If the owners hit the dates below, the realistic path is a limited beta for about 30 adjusters on **Mon 16 Nov** and all 300 by **Mon 14 Dec**.

## Why the one fraud case matters more than the 93%

- **The rate is small but uncertain.** 1 in 240 = 0.42%. The exact 95% interval is 0.01% to 2.3%, so the eval can't rule out a rate of about 1 in 45.
- **The slice is what matters.** The useful number is failures per fraud-flagged claim in the set, not per 240. If the set held only a handful of flagged claims, this failure is a large share of that slice. Report how many fraud-flagged claims the 240 contained.
- **"The adjuster decides" is weaker than it sounds.** With 300 adjusters and a tool that agrees 93% of the time, suggestions get accepted by habit (automation bias). Fast-track queues are built for light review. So the human check is the control most likely to fail exactly when you need it.
- **The fix belongs outside the model.** Add a deterministic guard: any claim with a fraud indicator (SIU referral, rules-engine flag, fraud score above threshold) can never get a fast-track suggestion and goes to SIU or standard review. Enforce it in code after the model runs, and test it with unit tests. A rule that must never be broken should be a rule, not a prompt. Also tell adjusters clearly that the assistant is **not** a fraud control.
- **Check the other disagreements for the same pattern.** About 16–18 cases disagreed (93% of 240 is 222–224 agreements). Find out which way they went. A severe or vulnerable-claimant claim pushed down in priority is far worse than one pushed up, and may also count as a critical criterion.

## Eval arithmetic

| Measure | Input | Result | Policy (high) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Margin of error | ±1.96 × √(0.93 × 0.07 / 240) | ±3.2 points → 95% CI ≈ 89.8%–96.2% | — |
| Pass rate | 93% (point estimate) | Below threshold | ≥ 95% |
| Golden set size | 240 | 60 cases short | ≥ 300 |
| Critical failures | 1 | Blocks | 0 |
| Runs per case | Not stated | Unknown | ≥ 3 |
| Fairness slices | Not stated | Missing | Required |
| Adversarial slice | Not done | Missing | Required |

**There is no baseline yet.** Agreement with senior adjusters only means something next to two other numbers on the same cases:
- How often today's frontline adjusters agree with seniors. This is the process the AI has to match or beat.
- How often seniors agree with each other. This is the ceiling on the labels.

If seniors agree with each other only about 90% of the time, a 95% "agreement" bar can't be reached. Fix the metric, for example by scoring against labels adjudicated by two seniors. Don't lower the bar. That choice belongs to the AI governance board.

## Risk tier basis

| Rule | Why it triggers | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| H-01 | Triage influences how insurance claims are handled and paid, which affects access to insurance | Stated fact. On its own it makes the tier High |
| H-02 | Claims usually contain health, injury or financial-account data | Assumption |
| H-03 | Claims handling is a regulated process | Assumption |
| L-03 | Claimant personal data | Stated fact |

- **Unanswered questions:** `vulnerable_users`, `third_party_model_provider`, `uses_retrieval`, `max_financial_impact_per_action`. Answering them can only keep or raise the tier. If any claim routed to fast-track is worth ≥1,000, H-05 also triggers.
- **Autonomy:** L1 Suggest, within the high-tier launch cap of L3. That is the right level; don't plan auto-routing. Moving up a level requires ≥500 reviewed actions, an override rate under 2% for ≥4 weeks, zero critical incidents, a working reversal path, and sign-off from all six approvers. Fast-track payment should never become automatic without its own gate review.
- **Calculator output:** 21 required controls (20 for the tier, plus HUM-01 at L1) and 6 approvers (product owner, engineering lead, security lead, privacy officer, legal counsel, AI governance board). Re-certification every 3 months.

## Gate status, G0–G3

| Gate | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| G0 Fit | Not evidenced | Triaging free-text claims is a reasonable fit for AI. The hard constraints (fraud flags, severity rules, regulatory deadlines) belong in deterministic rules wrapped around the model. |
| G1 Value | Not provided | No business case or unit costs were shared, so none were computed. This doesn't block shadow mode; it is needed before ramp. |
| G2 Quality | Not met | Below threshold, one critical failure, no baseline, critical criteria not defined. |
| G3 Risk and controls | Partial | Tier computed here. Risk register, fairness evaluation, red-team testing and control evidence are missing. |

## 1. Readiness checklist

"Not met (no evidence)" means the item may exist, but nothing was shown. Evidence closes it.

| Area | Item | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quality | Held-out eval at or above the tier thresholds | Not met | 93% on 240 against a bar of ≥95% on ≥300; held-out status and runs per case unknown |
| Quality | Zero critical failures | **Not met** | Fraud-flagged claim suggested for fast-track payment |
| Quality | Baseline comparison complete | Not met | No frontline-vs-senior or senior-vs-senior agreement on the same cases |
| Quality | Model judge calibrated | N/A | Scored as label agreement against senior adjusters; no model judge (assumed) |
| Safety and security | Red-team testing as the tier requires (EVAL-02) | **Not met** | Not done |
| Safety and security | Prompt-injection tests passed (SEC-01) | **Not met** | Not tested; claim narratives and attachments are untrusted, claimant-written input |
| Safety and security | Output handling reviewed (SEC-03) | Not met (no evidence) | Output should be limited to valid priority and queue values and checked before display |
| Controls | Every required and conditional control evidenced | Not met | Evidence exists only for OPS-01 (partly, the dashboard) and HUM-01 (by design) |
| User experience | AI disclosure (TRN-01) | Not met (no evidence) | Adjusters must see the suggestion labelled as AI. Whether claimants must be told is for legal |
| User experience | Error, refusal and low-confidence states | Not met (no evidence) | If the model is unsure or down, show "No suggestion, triage manually", never a default queue |
| User experience | Feedback mechanism | Not met (no evidence) | One-click "wrong priority / wrong queue" with a reason |
| User experience | Undo or appeal path (TRN-02, high tier) | Not met (no evidence) | Claimants can contest how their claim was handled and get a human review; adjusters can re-route |
| Operations | Dashboards and alerts with owners | Partly met | Dashboard ready; alert thresholds and owners not stated |
| Operations | Runbook (OPS-04) | Not met (no evidence) | — |
| Operations | Kill switch tested (OPS-02) | **Not met** | Built, never tested |
| Operations | Fallback path tested | Not met (no evidence) | Confirm manual triage is still staffed and working |
| Operations | Rate and spend limits | Not met (no evidence) | — |
| Operations | Model version pinned (OPS-05) | Not met (no evidence) | — |
| Support and communications | Support briefed; limitations documented; communications ready | Not met (no evidence) | 300 adjusters need training on what the tool is not (a fraud check) and how to override |
| Approvals | All six roles required by the policy have signed | **Not met** | Legal has not reviewed; the other five approvals are not evidenced |

## 2. Blocking gaps (No-go items)

| Gap | Why it blocks | Shortest path to closing it | Owner (role) | Target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Critical failure: fraud-flagged claim → fast-track | Policy allows 0 critical failures; it is a direct route to fraud losses | Build the deterministic fraud guard, with unit tests showing every flagged claim is blocked. Find the root cause (was the flag in the input?). Add an oversampled fraud-flagged slice and re-run with zero fast-track suggestions. | ML lead + SIU lead | Guard Fri 23 Oct; slice Fri 6 Nov |
| Eval below bar; no baseline | 93% < 95%; 240 < 300; no comparison with today's process | Expand to ≥300 held-out cases from shadow traffic. Oversample fraud-flagged, high-severity and injury, large-loss, vulnerable-claimant and each line of business. Two seniors label ≥20% of cases. Define the critical criteria. Run each case 3×. Measure frontline and senior-vs-senior agreement on the same set. | ML lead + claims QA lead | Fri 13 Nov |
| No red-team or prompt-injection testing | EVAL-02 and SEC-01 are mandatory, and claimants have a motive to attack | Red-team built around fraud: instructions planted in narratives, attachments and OCR text; disguised fraud indicators; attempts to force a "fast-track" suggestion. Confirm input is treated as data and output stays limited to valid values. Fix and re-test. | Security lead | Fri 6 Nov |
| Kill switch and fallback untested | An untested kill switch is a No-go on its own (OPS-02) | Drill it in production during the first week of shadow, which affects no one: switch off, time how long until suggestions stop (proposed limit ≤5 min), confirm claims flow to manual triage with none stuck, switch back on, record it. | Engineering lead + claims operations lead | Fri 30 Oct |
| Legal review and approvals | GOV-03: all six roles must sign before adjusters see output | Send legal the pack now: this review, the eval report, the data flow, intended use and jurisdictions. Legal decides regulatory status and what claimants must be told or allowed to contest. Collect all six sign-offs. | Product owner | Fri 13 Nov (depends on legal capacity) |
| No fairness evaluation | EVAL-03 is required at the high tier | Break agreement down by line of business, claim type, region or postcode band, claimant language and channel on the ≥300 set. Agree a maximum gap. | ML lead | Fri 13 Nov |
| Controls with no evidence | Every mandatory control needs evidence | Provide evidence for PRV-01 (DPIA), PRV-02, PRV-03, TRN-02, OPS-03, OPS-04, OPS-05, EVAL-04, GOV-01, alert owners and adjuster training. Some may already exist. | Product owner (collects); privacy officer, engineering lead | Fri 13 Nov |

## 3. Conditions (shadow stage only)

The decision for adjuster-visible launch is No-go. These conditions apply only to running shadow mode on Monday.

| Condition | Owner (role) | Due | Must close before stage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Suggestions are hidden from all 300 adjusters, verified in the production UI; output is only logged | Engineering lead | Fri 23 Oct | Shadow |
| Privacy officer confirms the lawful basis and DPIA scope for processing live claims data, and that vendor terms cover it (no training use; retention and residency acceptable) | Privacy officer | Fri 23 Oct | Shadow |
| Audit log of inputs and outputs is on, access-restricted, with retention set. Security lead confirms the model has no tools and no egress beyond the model endpoint | Engineering lead + security lead | Fri 23 Oct | Shadow |
| AI governance board explicitly approves the shadow stage. The policy has no reduced approval path for shadow, so the board decides | AI governance board | Fri 23 Oct | Shadow |

If the privacy confirmation isn't in by Friday, shadow mode moves too. There is no workaround for processing live claims data.

## 4. Rollout plan

| Stage | Exposure | Entry date | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| Internal dogfood | Merged with shadow: claims QA and a small panel of senior adjusters review logged suggestions daily | Mon 26 Oct | No open critical issues; disagreement categories triaged |
| Shadow | AI runs on every new claim; output hidden from adjusters | Mon 26 Oct | ≥3 weeks. ≥300 senior-adjudicated live claims (stratified) at ≥95%, 3 runs per case. Zero critical failures. Fairness gap within the agreed limit. Kill-switch and fallback drill passed. Red-team fixes re-tested. All six sign-offs in. |
| Limited beta | About 30 adjusters (10%), 1–2 teams | Mon 16 Nov | 2 weeks. Weekly sample of ≥100 reviewed claims at ≥95%. Zero critical incidents. Override rate within tolerance of the shadow disagreement rate. |
| Ramp | 25% (75 adjusters) on Mon 30 Nov, then 50% (150) on Mon 7 Dec | Mon 30 Nov | ≥1 week per step with no rollback trigger fired |
| General availability | All 300 adjusters | Mon 14 Dec | Hand over to G5. Re-certify every 3 months |

## 5. Pre-committed rollback triggers

The thresholds are proposals. Agree and sign them before the beta, so nobody explains away bad numbers afterwards.

| Trigger | Threshold | Action | Owner (role) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fraud-flagged claim gets a fast-track suggestion (the guard failed) | Any one | Kill switch; incident review. SEV1 if a payment was made | Engineering lead + SIU lead |
| Severe or vulnerable-claimant claim suggested at lowest priority and accepted | Any confirmed case | Pause rollout; add the case to the eval set; review | Claims QA lead |
| Weekly sampled agreement (≥100 claims) | <95% → hold ramp; <90% → kill switch | As stated | Product owner |
| Override rate | Above the shadow disagreement rate + 3 points for 3 working days in a row | Pause ramp; investigate | Product owner |
| Automation-bias signal | Acceptance >98% while sampled agreement is <95% | Pause ramp; refresher training; review the UX | Claims operations lead |
| Segment gap | >5 points between any two monitored segments | Pause ramp; fairness review | ML lead |
| Prompt injection | Any confirmed injection that changed a suggestion | Kill switch; security incident | Security lead |
| Availability or latency | Suggestions down, or p95 over budget, for >1 hour | Automatic fallback to manual triage; alert | Engineering lead |
| Cost per completed task | N/A — no budget supplied. Add once the business case exists | — | Product owner |

## 6. Sign-off

| Role | Decision | Date |
|---|---|---|
| Product owner | Pending | — |
| Engineering lead | Pending | — |
| Security lead | Pending (red team outstanding) | — |
| Privacy officer | Pending (needed for shadow by Fri 23 Oct) | — |
| Legal counsel | Not reviewed | — |
| AI governance board | Pending (shadow approval by Fri 23 Oct) | — |

## Regulatory flags (not legal advice; route to legal counsel and compliance)

- **Insurance sector rules.** Claims handling is regulated in most markets, including rules on fair and timely claims settlement. Regulators also have their own AI expectations. In the US, for example, the NAIC model bulletin on insurers' use of AI systems, adopted by many states, expects governance, testing for unfair discrimination and oversight of third parties.
- **EU AI Act.** It lists some insurance uses (risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance) as high-risk. Whether claims triage is in scope is for legal to decide.
- **GDPR.** Claims often include health data (special category), so a DPIA is likely. If adjusters' review becomes a rubber stamp, the automated-decision rules (Art. 22) may come into play.
- **UK.** FCA expectations on fair customer outcomes cover claims handling.
- **Jurisdictions unknown.** Legal needs to know which markets these claims come from.

## Assumptions Ledger

| Assumption | Why it matters | How to verify | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| The 93% covers priority and queue combined | A per-field rate could hide a weak field | Eval report broken down by field | ML lead |
| The 240 claims were held out from prompt tuning | If not, 93% is optimistic | Eval-set version and tuning log | ML lead |
| Each case ran once | The policy needs ≥3 runs with mean and spread | Re-run 3× | ML lead |
| Fraud indicators are structured fields at triage time | Needed for a deterministic guard | Check the data schema | SIU lead |
| Claims contain health and financial data | Triggers H-02 and the DPIA | Data inventory | Privacy officer |
| The model reads free text and attachments | Sets the prompt-injection surface | Data-flow diagram | Security lead |
| It only suggests and never writes to queues or payments | If it writes, SEC-02 and more audit duties apply | Architecture review | Engineering lead |
| An external model provider may be used | PRV-03 vendor terms | Vendor record | Privacy officer |
| Claim values routed to fast-track can be ≥1,000 | Triggers H-05 | Claims data | Claims operations lead |
| Manual triage is still staffed as the fallback | The kill switch is useless without it | Fallback drill | Claims operations lead |
| The dashboard covers quality, safety, cost and latency | OPS-01 needs alerts and owners | Dashboard and alert config | Engineering lead |
| No approver has signed yet | GOV-03 | Sign-off record | Product owner |
| Legal, engineering and security can meet the target dates | The beta and GA dates depend on them | Confirm with each owner this week | Product owner |

## Open decisions

| Decision | Owner role | Needed by |
|---|---|---|
| Accept shadow mode on Mon 26 Oct instead of an adjuster-visible launch | Product owner + AI governance board | Wed 21 Oct |
| Which fraud indicators hard-block fast-track | SIU lead + claims operations lead | Thu 22 Oct |
| Approve the shadow stage under the policy | AI governance board | Fri 23 Oct |
| Define "correct" for triage, the critical criteria and how disagreements are adjudicated | Claims operations lead + ML lead | Fri 30 Oct |
| What claimants must be told, and how they contest | Legal counsel + privacy officer | Fri 13 Nov |
| Sign the rollback thresholds | Product owner + claims operations lead | Fri 13 Nov |
| Business case and cost budget | Product owner | Mon 30 Nov (before ramp) |

**Next gate:** G4 re-review before the limited beta (target Fri 13 Nov). Complete the G3 risk assessment with it. G5 Operate and improve starts at GA.

trials.response:
## Bottom line

Don't switch providers this week. Treat the drop as a production incident and give yourselves 3 to 5 days to find the root cause. A 14-point fall in acceptance tells you something changed. It does not tell you the model is what changed. In most drops like this the cause is something else: what goes into the model, the mix of tickets, the product around it, or how acceptance is measured. If you switch before you know, you take on a migration, a vendor review and a prompt rewrite all at once. And if the cause was elsewhere, the drop moves to the new provider with you.

Start evaluating the other provider now, alongside the diagnosis, so you have the option ready if the model does turn out to be the problem.

## Why switching this week is the wrong move

- **The new setup is untested.** Your prompts, retrieval formatting and guardrails were tuned for the current model. A different model running the same prompts often does worse at first.
- **It muddies the diagnosis.** If acceptance moves after the switch, you won't know whether the switch caused it or the real cause got better or worse by itself.
- **It skips governance.** A new provider handling customer support data (which includes PII) needs a vendor risk and security review, a DPA, and checks on retention, residency and training-on-your-data terms. Doing that in a week is a compliance exposure.
- **It may fix nothing.** If the cause is a stale knowledge base (KB), a broken retrieval index or a shift in ticket mix, a new model will be wrong in the same way.

## Days 0 to 1: confirm the drop and find when it started

1. **Check the metric is real.** Did the acceptance event, its definition (for example, "accepted then heavily edited" now counted as a reject), the denominator (suggestions now shown on more queues, or generated but not displayed) or the client build change? Check that logging is complete. Confirm that 62 to 48 is outside normal day-to-day variance at your volume, and allow for day-of-week effects.
2. **Look at the shape of the drop.** Plot acceptance daily, or hourly. A step change on one date points to a deploy, a config change or a model version change. A gradual slide points to ticket mix, content going stale, or agent behavior.
3. **Build a change log for the last 14 days.** Cover:
   - **Model:** are you pinned to a dated version, or on an alias the provider can update silently? Check the provider's changelog and status page.
   - **Your pipeline:** prompt or template, temperature and max tokens, retrieval, embeddings, index refresh, CRM or context fields, safety filters.
   - **Content:** KB articles or policies that changed (pricing, refunds, a product launch).
   - **Operations:** UI changes, routing, new queues or languages, new hires or a new BPO site, new QA guidance, and any incident or launch that brought in new kinds of ticket.
4. **Check operational health.** Look at p50 and p95 latency, since agents ignore a suggestion that arrives after they've started typing. Also check timeouts, errors, empty or cut-off outputs, and refusals from the content filter.

## Days 2 to 3: isolate the cause

1. **Break the drop down by segment.** Split acceptance by queue, intent, language, channel, product, and agent tenure or site. Then separate the mix effect from the rate effect. If acceptance within each segment held steady and only the mix moved, the model didn't get worse: you're seeing ticket types it handles less well.
2. **Read the rejected suggestions.** Sample 150 to 200 of them from before and after the drop, spread across segments. Have two or three senior agents or QA reviewers tag why each was rejected:
   - factually wrong
   - outdated policy
   - missing customer context
   - wrong tone or length
   - irrelevant
   - made up
   - fine, but the agent preferred their own reply

   A change in which reasons dominate usually points to the cause within a day.
3. **Replay tickets to separate the model from its inputs.** This is the one test that answers "did the model get worse?" Take a fixed set of post-drop tickets and run them through two setups:
   - today's production pipeline
   - the pipeline as it was before the drop: old prompt, old config, an index snapshot, and the old model version if you can still get it

   Keep the inputs the same and change one component at a time. Score the outputs against a rubric, either human-graded or with an LLM judge you've checked against human grades.
4. **Re-run your frozen golden set** against today's production. If scores match the baseline, the model is fine on known cases, and the problem is new or changed inputs.

## Decision table

| Finding | Action | Switch provider? |
|---|---|---|
| Instrumentation or definition change | Fix the metric and reset the baseline | No |
| Ticket mix shift (launch, outage, new queue or language) | Add KB content and prompt handling for the new intents. Turn suggestions off in segments below a quality threshold | No |
| KB or policy changed, retrieval stale or broken, context fields missing | Fix the pipeline, rebuild the index, add freshness checks | No |
| Latency or timeouts | Fix infrastructure, stream responses, set a latency SLO | No |
| Our own prompt or config change | Roll it back | No |
| Provider silently updated the model behind an alias | Pin the previous dated version, open a support case with your replay evidence, require version pinning from now on | Not yet. This triggers a formal evaluation |
| Same inputs and prompt, current model measurably worse, and you can't pin back | Escalate to the provider and fast-track the alternative through the gates below | Possibly, through the gated process |
| Agent behavior changed (new QA rule, new hires, incentives) | Training, UX fixes, align the QA guidance | No |

## Evaluate the alternative in parallel, with gates

Starting the evaluation now is sensible because it gives you a real option. Switching production should still require all of the following:

- **Offline win.** The candidate beats the current model on the golden set and on the post-drop replay set by a margin you agree in advance (for example, 5 or more points of rubric pass rate). It must not regress on high-stakes categories (refunds, billing, legal or compliance wording), safety, tone, or PII handling.
- **Latency and cost.** p95 latency and cost per suggestion stay within budget.
- **Approvals.** Vendor risk, security and legal sign-off: DPA, retention, no training on your data, residency.
- **Shadow, then canary.** Randomize 5 to 10% of agents for 1 to 2 weeks, with success metrics registered in advance:
  - **Success metrics:** acceptance, edit distance, handle time, QA score or CSAT, and how often customers contact you again about the same issue.
  - **Guardrail metrics:** factual error rate and escalations.
- **Rollback plan.** A tested way back to the current provider.

Expect 3 to 6 weeks for this, not one.

## Check the metric that matters more

Acceptance is a proxy. When acceptance falls while agents are still reviewing every suggestion, it can mean the human review step is working and catching bad suggestions. The bigger risk is wrong suggestions that agents accept and send, such as outdated refund terms. Check QA scores on replies built from accepted suggestions, how heavily accepted suggestions get edited, and complaints or repeat contacts. If wrong information is reaching customers, mitigate now: turn suggestions off for the affected intents and warn agents.

## What to tell the team today

"We're treating this as an incident. [Name] owns it, and we'll have the root cause by [date, 3 to 5 days out]. We're starting an offline evaluation of [provider] now, so if the model is the problem we won't be starting from zero. We won't switch production providers until the evidence shows the model is the cause and the alternative wins on our evals and in a canary."

Owners:

- **PM:** runs the incident and owns the decision.
- **ML engineering:** replay and golden set.
- **Data or analytics:** segmentation and the mix-versus-rate breakdown.
- **Support operations:** the change log and tagging rejected suggestions.
- **Vendor management:** the provider support case and the new vendor's review.

## Prevent the next one

- Pin dated model versions. Treat any version change as a release that has to pass a golden-set regression test.
- Put prompts, retrieval and KB changes through change control and release gates.
- Monitor and alert on:
  - acceptance by segment
  - latency
  - empty or cut-off outputs
  - how often retrieval finds relevant content
  - KB freshness
  - drift in the ticket intent mix
- Track quality beyond acceptance: edit distance, and QA scores on a sample of sent replies.
- Keep a provider abstraction layer and a maintained eval harness. Then a future switch takes days and rests on evidence, instead of a week of guessing.

trials.response:
**Verdict: Don't switch providers this week. Run the regression protocol and decide by Fri 2026-10-23 · Provisional severity: SEV2 · Risk tier: Limited · Policy: aipg-default v1.1.0 (bundled default)**

## The short answer

A 14-point drop is almost certainly real. That doesn't mean the model got worse. When a team reports that "the model got worse", the cause is usually something else: a change in how the metric is measured, a deploy, a change in the traffic, or a broken dependency (most often a stale knowledge base). Switching provider now would:

1. **Probably not fix it.** If the cause is the metric, the ticket mix, the knowledge base, latency or the UI, the new model inherits it.
2. **Destroy the evidence.** If you change the biggest variable mid-investigation, you lose the before/after comparison you need to find the cause.
3. **Start you behind.** Prompts rarely transfer unchanged. A new model running your current prompt usually scores below a tuned incumbent until someone re-tunes the prompt.
4. **Break policy.** At Limited tier a new provider is a material change. It needs:
   - an evaluated, staged release (OPS-05)
   - a golden-set eval (EVAL-01)
   - a vendor data-terms review before customer data reaches the new vendor (PRV-03)
   - injection and red-team tests (SEC-01, EVAL-02)
   - sign-off from the Product owner, Engineering lead, Security lead and Privacy officer
   - re-certification (GOV-02)

   That doesn't fit in a week, and doing it badly is worse than not doing it.

**What to do instead:**
- Spend 4 working days on the diagnosis below.
- Roll back anything that changed when the drop started.
- Start the new vendor's paperwork in parallel. It doesn't touch production, so if the evidence does point at the model, you've lost no time.

The team still gets a decision this week, based on evidence.

## What the numbers already tell you

| Measure | Working | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute drop | 62% − 48% = **14 points** | Large. Not a rounding-error change. |
| Relative drop | 14 ÷ 62 = **22.6%** | About 1 in 4.4 previously accepted suggestions is now rejected. |
| Is it noise? | 95% margin for the gap between two rates = 1.96 × √(p₁(1−p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1−p₂)/n₂). With p₁ = 0.62 and p₂ = 0.48: ±6.1 points at 500 suggestions per window, ±11.1 at 150, ±13.7 at 100. | Unless each window had fewer than about 100–150 suggestions, the drop is not noise. Confirm the counts. Real in the metric is not the same as caused by the model. |
| Model cost per accepted suggestion | Cost per accepted suggestion = cost per suggestion ÷ acceptance rate. The ratio is (1 ÷ 0.48) ÷ (1 ÷ 0.62) = 0.62 ÷ 0.48 = **1.29** | Each useful suggestion now costs **29% more** in model spend. That is above the 20% cost alert in the Gate 5 monitoring plan and the "more than 20%" re-evaluation trigger for model decisions. This justifies re-evaluating, and the protocol is how you re-evaluate. Agent time rises too, because every rejected suggestion is a reply written from scratch. |

**Why the traffic mix matters (illustrative numbers, not your data).** Overall acceptance = Σ (segment share × segment acceptance). Suppose existing ticket types still accept at 62%, and a new ticket type accepts at 20% and has grown to a third of volume. Overall acceptance is then ⅔ × 62% + ⅓ × 20% = **48.0%**. That is your exact drop, with no change to the model at all.

## Regression review: support-reply suggestion acceptance drop (62% → 48%)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Feature | AI support-reply suggestions (agent assist) |
| Type | Quality regression |
| Severity | **SEV2 (provisional):** a systematic quality failure affecting many users, with no confirmed harm. Upgrade to **SEV1** if any accepted suggestion sent harmful, unlawful or data-exposing content to a customer. |
| Owner (role) | Product owner (accountable); ML lead (runs the diagnosis) |
| Detected | To confirm. The drop began about 2026-10-09, 10 days before 2026-10-19. |
| Contained | N/A so far. Agents review every suggestion before sending (L2), which limits customer exposure. The harm check on 2026-10-20 confirms or rules this out. |
| Policy | aipg-default v1.1.0 (bundled default). Re-run the tier if your organisation has its own `.ai-governance/policy.json`. |

**Governance context.** Running the risk tier calculator on the assumptions in the ledger returns **Limited**, triggered by three rules:
- L-01: replies reach customers.
- L-03: tickets contain personal data.
- L-04: that data goes to an external model provider.

Two conditional controls also apply: HUM-01, because a human reviews every output at L2, and PRV-04, if suggestions use retrieval. Limited-tier minimums: a golden set of at least 150 cases, a pass rate of at least 90%, zero critical failures, at least 3 runs per case, a weekly human-review sample of at least 50, and re-certification every 6 months.

This review is blameless: it looks at systems and signals, not individuals.

### 1. Summary
Support agents' acceptance of AI reply suggestions fell from 62% to 48% over about 10 days. Agents are rejecting more suggestions, which costs them time. No customer harm is confirmed, because agents review every suggestion before sending. The diagnosis is under way, and the provider switch is on hold until the regression protocol below is complete.

### 2. Impact
| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Users or records affected | Every agent using suggestions. Suggestion count in the window: to pull. |
| Duration | About 10 days, ongoing |
| Harm (data exposure, wrong actions, financial, reputational) | **Productivity:** 14 fewer accepted suggestions per 100 shown. **Model spend:** +29% per accepted suggestion (0.62 ÷ 0.48). **Customer harm:** none confirmed yet. Check the replies that were accepted and sent: a QA sample, reopen rate, CSAT and complaints since about 2026-10-09. |
| Notifications made (privacy, legal, security, customers) | None needed at SEV2. Notify the privacy, legal and security owners only if the harm check finds data exposure or harmful output (SEV1). |

### 3. Timeline
| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| ≈ 2026-09-11 to 2026-10-08 | Baseline of about 62%. Confirm this is a stable four-week baseline, not a peak. |
| ≈ 2026-10-09 | Drop begins. Confirm whether it is a **step change** on one day (points to step 2) or a **gradual slide** (points to steps 3 and 4). |
| 2026-10-19 | Provider switch proposed; regression review opened; change freeze starts |
| 2026-10-20 | Steps 1 and 2 done; anything that lines up with the drop is rolled back |
| 2026-10-21 | Steps 3 and 4 done |
| 2026-10-22 | Step 5 replay and golden-set comparison done |
| 2026-10-23 | Decision review: fix, pin or re-prompt, or open a model decision record for a switch |

### 4. Diagnosis (regression protocol, in order)

Work through these steps in order. Steps 1 to 4 are mostly data queries and can run in parallel across two people.

| Step | What to check | Fast tell | If confirmed | Share of the drop explained |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Measurement and instrumentation** | Plot the numerator (accepted) and the denominator (shown) separately. Check whether the definition of "accepted" changed, for example accept-then-edit or copy-paste now counted differently. Look for a help-desk or client release that broke event logging, an uninstrumented new insert button, suggestions now shown on ticket types that were excluded before, duplicate impression events, and test or bot traffic. | "Shown" jumped while "accepted" stayed flat. | Fix the logging, re-baseline, and diagnose only what remains. | TBD |
| **2. Change log** (prompt, model, retrieval, tools, configuration) | List everything that changed in the 2 weeks before the drop: prompt, model version or alias, provider routing or region, retrieval index or knowledge-base content, macros, guardrails and filters, temperature and max tokens, the help-desk UI, the agent workflow. Check whether the model version string in your API responses changed. Overlay deploy times on the daily chart. | The drop starts at a deploy timestamp. | Roll the change back. It is cheap and reversible, and the rollback is itself the test: if acceptance recovers within 1–2 days, you've found the cause. A moving unpinned "latest" alias is the one real "the model got worse" case, and the fix is to **pin the version**, not to switch provider. | TBD |
| **3. Input mix** | Break acceptance down by intent or ticket category, language, channel, product, customer tier, and agent team and tenure. Agent mix is often missed: new hires, a newly onboarded outsourced team, or new QA guidance can change acceptance with no model change at all. Decompose the change: Δ overall = Σ (Δ share × old rate) [mix effect] + Σ (new share × Δ rate) [within-segment effect]. Look for a product launch, an outage, a pricing or policy change, a campaign, or a new market. | Stable segments are flat, and the mix moved. | The cause is the mix, not the model. Improve coverage for the new segment (knowledge-base articles, examples), or stop showing suggestions there until that segment meets the bar. | TBD |
| **4. Dependencies** | Retrieval: do rejected suggestions cite outdated policies, prices or procedures? Did a knowledge-base article change without a re-index, or did the index job fail? Check the empty-retrieval rate. Latency: did p95 time-to-suggestion rise? If suggestions arrive after the agent has started typing, acceptance falls even when the content is fine. Also check timeouts that truncate long threads, rate limiting, how often the fallback path activates, and missing CRM fields. | Rejected suggestions contain stale facts, or p95 latency, timeouts or fallback use went up. | Fix the dependency. Give each knowledge source a named owner and a re-index cadence. | TBD |
| **5. Model behaviour** (replay against last-known-good) | Take a fixed, stratified sample of 200–300 recent tickets, over-weighting rejected suggestions and the segments that dropped. Run it through (a) the current setup and (b) the last-known-good setup: pinned model version, prompt and index snapshot from before 2026-10-09. Run the golden set on both, with at least 150 cases and at least 3 runs per case, graded with the existing rubric. At 150 cases and a 90% pass rate the margin is ±4.8 points, so treat smaller gaps as unproven. In parallel, have two senior agents tag reasons on about 50 rejected suggestions from the last 10 days and about 50 from before: wrong facts or policy, irrelevant, wrong tone, too long, not needed. Policy requires a weekly human-review sample of at least 50 (HUM-03). If that log exists, read it first; it may already answer the question. | Last-known-good beats current **on the same inputs, with everything else held constant**. | The model is implicated. Apply the decision rule in section 5. | TBD |

Causes often stack (for example, part mix, part stale knowledge base, part logging). Put a number on each cause's share before you act, so the fix you choose covers the whole drop.

### 5. Root cause and contributing factors
Pending the protocol. **Pre-commit the decision rule now**, so nobody has to argue it after the numbers come in:

| If the protocol finds… | Do this | Switch provider? |
|---|---|---|
| A change in measurement | Fix the logging and re-baseline | No |
| A change shipped in the window (prompt, index, configuration, UI) | Roll back or fix that change | No |
| A shift in the input mix | Improve coverage for the new segment, or suppress suggestions there | No |
| A dependency (stale knowledge base, latency, timeouts, fallback) | Fix the dependency; assign a source owner and a re-index cadence | No |
| A model behaviour change from an unpinned alias or a provider-side version change | Pin the last-known-good version and enforce OPS-05 | Only if that version is unavailable or deprecated |
| A model behaviour change that pinning and prompt fixes can't bring back to the bar | Open a model decision record and evaluate candidates | **Yes, as a candidate**, through the change path below |

**Change path if a switch is warranted.** Fill in the model decision record template and require all of the following:

| Criterion | Bar |
|---|---|
| Golden set | The same eval-set version for the incumbent's last-known-good setup and every candidate; at least 150 cases and at least 3 runs per case |
| Pass rate | At least 90%, and at least as good as the last-known-good setup |
| Critical failures | 0. Examples: an invented policy, price or refund promise; another customer's data in a reply |
| Cost per completed task | From `unit_economics.py`, using each candidate's prices and **its measured acceptance rate** as `success_rate`, not price per token |
| p95 latency | Within the time-to-suggestion budget at expected concurrency |
| Data terms (PRV-03) | Training use, retention, residency and the processor contract reviewed. The Privacy officer and legal counsel should check whether GDPR Art. 28 (processors) and Chapter V (transfers) apply if EU customer data is involved. This is a flag for review, not a legal conclusion. |
| Security | SEC-01 prompt-injection tests and EVAL-02 red-team run on the new model. Customer messages are untrusted input. |
| Rollout | Shadow on live traffic, then 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%. Agree rollback triggers before you start, for example acceptance below the incumbent for 2 consecutive days at any stage, or any critical failure. |
| Approvals | Product owner, Engineering lead, Security lead, Privacy officer; then re-certification (GOV-02) |

### 6. Actions
| Action | Type (fix / detect / prevent) | Owner (role) | Due | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Freeze prompt, model, index and configuration changes on this feature, except rollbacks | Prevent | Engineering lead | 2026-10-19 | Open |
| Harm check on suggestions accepted and sent since about 2026-10-09: QA sample, reopen rate, complaints | Detect | Support QA lead | 2026-10-20 | Open |
| Steps 1–2: audit the metric; overlay the change log on the daily chart | Fix | Engineering lead | 2026-10-20 | Open |
| Roll back any change that lines up with the drop | Fix | Engineering lead | 2026-10-20 | Open |
| Steps 3–4: segment decomposition and dependency check | Fix | Data/analytics lead with ML lead | 2026-10-21 | Open |
| Step 5: replay against last-known-good; golden set on both; label rejection reasons | Fix | ML lead | 2026-10-22 | Open |
| Decision review using the rule in section 5 | Fix | Product owner | 2026-10-23 | Open |
| Start the PRV-03 vendor assessment and procurement for the shortlisted provider. No production traffic. | Prevent (removes lead time) | Privacy officer with procurement | Start 2026-10-20 | Open |
| Pin the exact model version and log it on every request | Prevent | Engineering lead | 2026-10-23 | Open |
| Add the failing cases to the eval set | Prevent | ML lead | Within 1 week of root cause | Open |
| Alert on acceptance against the four-week baseline, by segment | Detect | Product owner | 2026-10-30 | Open |
| Capture a reject reason in the UI (one tap, optional) | Detect | Product owner | 2026-11-06 | Open |
| Continuous eval (EVAL-04): run the golden set on every prompt, model, retrieval or tool change, and block releases below threshold | Prevent | ML lead | 2026-11-06 | Open |

### 7. Detection gap
A 10-day slide should page someone within 2–3 days. Add these:
- **An acceptance alert against the four-week baseline, by segment.** Start at "3-day rolling acceptance more than 5 points below baseline" and calibrate from there; this starting value is an assumption.
- **Deploy and knowledge-base change markers** on the quality dashboard.
- **The model version on every request**, so an alias change is visible.
- **A reject-reason capture**, so the "why" is already in the data.
- **The weekly HUM-03 sample of at least 50**, scored against the rubric.
- **EVAL-04 gating** on every change.

If any of these existed, this review would take one day instead of four.

## Assumptions Ledger
| Assumption | Why it matters | How to verify | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Agents review, edit and send every suggestion (L2 Draft); nothing goes to customers automatically | Sets the tier, the controls, and whether customer harm is contained | UX flow and event logs | Product owner |
| Tickets contain customer personal data, which goes to an external model provider | Triggers rules L-03 and L-04 and the PRV-03 review for any new vendor | Data flow diagram | Privacy officer |
| Suggestions use retrieval over a knowledge base or macros | Adds the PRV-04 control and makes step 4 a likely cause | Architecture review | Engineering lead |
| 62% is a stable four-week baseline, not a short-lived peak | If 62% was a spike, part of the "drop" is a return to normal | Daily series for the previous 6 weeks | Data/analytics lead |
| More than about 150 suggestions per window | Below that, a 14-point gap could be noise | Count suggestions shown per window | Data/analytics lead |
| The definition and logging of "accepted" are unchanged | If they changed, part or all of the drop is a measurement artifact | Step 1 audit | Engineering lead |
| No harmful or wrong content reached customers through accepted suggestions | Decides SEV2 versus SEV1, and whether containment and notifications are needed | QA sample, reopen rate, complaints | Support QA lead |
| The last-known-good setup (model version, prompt, index snapshot) can be reproduced | Step 5 depends on it | Config history and index snapshots | ML lead |
| A golden set of at least 150 cases with a rubric exists from launch | Without one, neither the replay nor a provider comparison is valid, and building it becomes the first blocking task | Eval repository and version | ML lead |
| A provider switch done to policy takes more than a week | This is the basis for not switching this week | Procurement and PRV-03 lead times | Privacy officer with procurement |
| The bundled default policy is the right one to apply | Your organisation's policy may set different tiers or controls | Check for `.ai-governance/policy.json` | AI governance board |

**Re-certification required:** **No** for the diagnosis or for rollbacks to the last-known-good state. **Yes** if the fix changes the model or provider, which is a material change under GOV-02 and OPS-05.

## Open decisions
| Decision | Owner role | Needed by |
|---|---|---|
| Approve the change freeze and a 2026-10-23 evidence-based decision in place of a switch this week | Product owner | 2026-10-19 |
| Confirm the severity (SEV2, or upgrade to SEV1) after the harm check | Product owner with Support QA lead | 2026-10-20 |
| Roll back any change that lines up with the drop | Engineering lead | 2026-10-20 |
| Start the vendor pre-qualification (PRV-03) in parallel | Product owner with Privacy officer | 2026-10-20 |
| Decide between fix, pin or re-prompt, and switch, on the evidence. A switch also needs the Engineering lead, Security lead and Privacy officer to sign off. | Product owner with ML lead | 2026-10-23 |
| Confirm whether an organisation policy file replaces the bundled default | AI governance board | 2026-10-23 |

## Next gate
- **Stay in Gate 5** until the root cause is fixed, verified on the golden set, and the failing cases are added to the eval set.
- **If the decision is to switch provider**, run these in order:
  1. Approach and model selection: model decision record comparing candidates on the same golden set.
  2. Gate 2: eval against the Limited-tier bar.
  3. Gate 3: re-run the risk tier for the new vendor, plus PRV-03, SEC-01 and EVAL-02.
  4. Gate 4: shadow, staged ramp and pre-committed rollback triggers.
  5. Re-certification.
